## Student Loan Bankruptcy in Colorado [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR
Source: https://bankruptcystudentloans.org/states/colorado.html

← bankruptcystudentloans.org home

Student Loan Bankruptcy in Colorado [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Colorado residents.

Student Loan Discharge in Colorado

Colorado sits in the Tenth Circuit, which applies the Brunner three-prong test. Each prong must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence in an adversary proceeding.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). To discharge them, the debtor must file an adversary proceeding within the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the test applied in the Tenth Circuit.

The Tenth Circuit Brunner Standard

Applies Brunner. In re Woodcock, 45 F.3d 363 (10th Cir. 1995). Recent panels have loosened the good-faith prong; see McDaniel v. Navient (2020) on tuition-vs-educational distinction.

Brunner (where it applies) requires the debtor to prove:

Minimal standard of living. That the debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and dependents if forced to repay the loans.

Persistence. That additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. That the debtor has made good faith efforts to repay the loans (including IDR/IBR enrollment, forbearances attempted, and payment history).

See the full Brunner test explanation.

DOJ/DOE Attestation Process (Nov 2022)

In November 2022, the Department of Justice and Department of Education issued joint guidance that streamlines student loan discharge for federal loans. The guidance applies in every federal court, including those in Colorado, and has materially increased discharge success rates.

Under the attestation process:

The debtor completes a standardized DOJ attestation form documenting income, expenses, and repayment history.

The DOJ reviews the attestation and, in most cases, supports discharge rather than contesting.

The underlying Brunner/totality analysis is applied, but with DOJ alignment.

The U.S. Trustee in Colorado processes adversary proceedings consistent with this guidance. See adversary proceeding mechanics.

Colorado Disability and TPD Discharge

Colorado Health Service Corps; federal TPD for disability. For Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) or Social Security Supplemental Security Income (SSI) recipients, federal loans qualify for Total and Permanent Disability (TPD) discharge without bankruptcy. TPD is administrative - no adversary proceeding needed - and applies to federal Direct, FFEL, and Perkins loans.

Three TPD qualification paths:

VA determination - Service-connected disability rated 100% or Individual Unemployability.

SSA determination - SSDI or SSI approval with a 5-7 year scheduled review flag.

Physician certification - M.D. or D.O. certifies that a medical impairment prevents substantial gainful activity.

TPD is the first path to check for any Colorado debtor with a disability. Bankruptcy discharge is the fallback when TPD is unavailable or for private loans.

Colorado Income-Driven Repayment Baseline

Before filing an adversary proceeding, most courts in the Tenth Circuit require the debtor to show they have attempted income-driven repayment (IDR). Denver metro IDR modeling benefits from elevated BLS housing allowance.

Federal IDR plans available:

SAVE (formerly REPAYE) - 5-10% of discretionary income; lowest monthly payments for most debtors.

PAYE - 10% of discretionary income; 20-year forgiveness.

IBR - 10-15% of discretionary income; 20-25 year forgiveness.

ICR - 20% of discretionary income or 12-year standard, whichever less.

A Colorado debtor at poverty-line income typically has a $0 monthly IDR payment under SAVE. This is important for the Brunner good-faith prong: you must show you tried IDR, not that IDR was impossible.

Private Student Loans in Colorado

Private student loans are treated differently. Under the 10th Circuit's McDaniel v. Navient, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020), and similar reasoning in other circuits, a "qualified education loan" under 523(a)(8)(B) requires the funds to have been used solely for qualified educational expenses. Loans for living expenses, test preparation, or bar study may be dischargeable without proving undue hardship.

For Colorado debtors with private loans:

Direct-to-consumer (DTC) loans - often exceed "cost of attendance" and may be fully dischargeable.

Bar study loans - typically dischargeable under In re Campbell / McDaniel reasoning.

Mixed-use loans - fact-specific; the burden is on the creditor to prove qualified-loan status.

See private student loan dischargeability.

Colorado Federal Bankruptcy Data

Student loan adversary proceedings are filed within an underlying Chapter 7 or 13 case. The Colorado consumer bankruptcy volume below shows the size of the pool where a 523(a)(8) complaint could be brought.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 86 consumer bankruptcy cases from Colorado's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 78498.8%1.2%

Chapter 132n/an/a

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Colorado Chapter 13 and Student Loans

In Chapter 13, student loans are generally paid pro-rata with other unsecured debt through the plan under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(1). The debtor may still file an adversary proceeding for discharge on undue hardship grounds, either during the case or after plan completion.

Practical advantages of the Chapter 13 path in Colorado:

The automatic stay halts collection during the 3-5 year plan.

Accrued interest may be reduced through plan treatment.

A post-plan discharge adversary may succeed where a pre-plan one would not, because a completed plan is strong good-faith evidence.

See Chapter 13 and student loans.

Attorney Fees for Colorado Adversary Proceedings

Student loan adversary proceedings carry fees in addition to the base Chapter 7 or 13 attorney fee. Typical Colorado range: $2,000-$6,000 depending on case complexity and whether the loan holder contests discharge.

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 329(b), the bankruptcy court may review any attorney fee paid "in connection with" the case, including adversary-proceeding fees. Any fee paid for student loan litigation must be disclosed under Rule 2016(b) and is subject to the reasonableness standard. See Section 329 fee disgorgement overview.

Related Colorado Resources

Adversary proceeding mechanics

Chapter 13 and student loans

Private student loans

Income-driven repayment

Student loan bankruptcy FAQ

Colorado bankruptcy exemptions

Section 329 fee disgorgement

Foundational Caselaw

The cases below define the doctrine on this site:

Brunner v. New York State Higher Educ. Servs. Corp., 831 F.2d 395 (2d Cir. 1987) - origin of the three-prong undue-hardship test (per curiam).

McDaniel v. Navient Solutions, LLC, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020) - private student loans outside Section 523(a)(8) scope.

Rosenberg v. New York State Higher Educ. Servs. Corp., 610 B.R. 454 (S.D.N.Y. 2020) - seminal post-Brunner critique; catalyst for the 2022 DOJ attestation guidance.

Long v. Educational Credit Mgmt. Corp., 322 F.3d 549 (8th Cir. 2003) - totality-of-circumstances alternative.

## Student Loan Bankruptcy in Connecticut [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR
Source: https://bankruptcystudentloans.org/states/connecticut.html

← bankruptcystudentloans.org home

Student Loan Bankruptcy in Connecticut [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Connecticut residents.

Student Loan Discharge in Connecticut

Connecticut sits in the Second Circuit, which applies the Brunner three-prong test. Each prong must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence in an adversary proceeding.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). To discharge them, the debtor must file an adversary proceeding within the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the test applied in the Second Circuit.

The Second Circuit Brunner Standard

Adopted Brunner originally (the test is named after a 2d Circuit case). Strict three-prong application. Brunner v. New York State Higher Educ. Servs. Corp., 831 F.2d 395 (2d Cir. 1987). Good-faith prong heavily scrutinized.

Brunner (where it applies) requires the debtor to prove:

Minimal standard of living. That the debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and dependents if forced to repay the loans.

Persistence. That additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. That the debtor has made good faith efforts to repay the loans (including IDR/IBR enrollment, forbearances attempted, and payment history).

See the full Brunner test explanation.

The debtor completes a standardized DOJ attestation form documenting income, expenses, and repayment history.

The DOJ reviews the attestation and, in most cases, supports discharge rather than contesting.

The underlying Brunner/totality analysis is applied, but with DOJ alignment.

Before filing an adversary proceeding, most courts in the Second Circuit require the debtor to show they have attempted income-driven repayment (IDR). High COL; meaningful IDR expense offset available.

Federal IDR plans available:

SAVE (formerly REPAYE) - 5-10% of discretionary income; lowest monthly payments for most debtors.

PAYE - 10% of discretionary income; 20-year forgiveness.

IBR - 10-15% of discretionary income; 20-25 year forgiveness.

ICR - 20% of discretionary income or 12-year standard, whichever less.

Minimal standard of living. That the debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and dependents if forced to repay the loans.

## Student Loan Bankruptcy in District of Columbia [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR
Source: https://bankruptcystudentloans.org/states/district-of-columbia.html

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for District of Columbia residents.

## Student Loan Bankruptcy in Florida [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR
Source: https://bankruptcystudentloans.org/states/florida.html

← bankruptcystudentloans.org home

Student Loan Bankruptcy in Florida [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Florida residents.

Student Loan Discharge in Florida

Florida sits in the Eleventh Circuit, which applies the Brunner three-prong test. Each prong must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence in an adversary proceeding.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). To discharge them, the debtor must file an adversary proceeding within the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the test applied in the Eleventh Circuit.

The Eleventh Circuit Brunner Standard

Applies Brunner. In re Cox, 338 F.3d 1238 (11th Cir. 2003). The Hemar Ins. Corp. v. Cox line has been influential on the second prong.

Brunner (where it applies) requires the debtor to prove:

Minimal standard of living. That the debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and dependents if forced to repay the loans.

Persistence. That additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. That the debtor has made good faith efforts to repay the loans (including IDR/IBR enrollment, forbearances attempted, and payment history).

See the full Brunner test explanation.

DOJ/DOE Attestation Process (Nov 2022)

In November 2022, the Department of Justice and Department of Education issued joint guidance that streamlines student loan discharge for federal loans. The guidance applies in every federal court, including those in Florida, and has materially increased discharge success rates.

Under the attestation process:

The debtor completes a standardized DOJ attestation form documenting income, expenses, and repayment history.

The DOJ reviews the attestation and, in most cases, supports discharge rather than contesting.

The underlying Brunner/totality analysis is applied, but with DOJ alignment.

The U.S. Trustee in Florida processes adversary proceedings consistent with this guidance. See adversary proceeding mechanics.

Florida Disability and TPD Discharge

Florida limited programs for nursing/teaching; federal TPD. For Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) or Social Security Supplemental Security Income (SSI) recipients, federal loans qualify for Total and Permanent Disability (TPD) discharge without bankruptcy. TPD is administrative - no adversary proceeding needed - and applies to federal Direct, FFEL, and Perkins loans.

Three TPD qualification paths:

VA determination - Service-connected disability rated 100% or Individual Unemployability.

SSA determination - SSDI or SSI approval with a 5-7 year scheduled review flag.

Physician certification - M.D. or D.O. certifies that a medical impairment prevents substantial gainful activity.

TPD is the first path to check for any Florida debtor with a disability. Bankruptcy discharge is the fallback when TPD is unavailable or for private loans.

Florida Income-Driven Repayment Baseline

Before filing an adversary proceeding, most courts in the Eleventh Circuit require the debtor to show they have attempted income-driven repayment (IDR). Low state income tax; but IDR only counts AGI, not state tax posture.

Federal IDR plans available:

SAVE (formerly REPAYE) - 5-10% of discretionary income; lowest monthly payments for most debtors.

PAYE - 10% of discretionary income; 20-year forgiveness.

IBR - 10-15% of discretionary income; 20-25 year forgiveness.

ICR - 20% of discretionary income or 12-year standard, whichever less.

A Florida debtor at poverty-line income typically has a $0 monthly IDR payment under SAVE. This is important for the Brunner good-faith prong: you must show you tried IDR, not that IDR was impossible.

Private Student Loans in Florida

Private student loans are treated differently. Under the 10th Circuit's McDaniel v. Navient, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020), and similar reasoning in other circuits, a "qualified education loan" under 523(a)(8)(B) requires the funds to have been used solely for qualified educational expenses. Loans for living expenses, test preparation, or bar study may be dischargeable without proving undue hardship.

For Florida debtors with private loans:

Direct-to-consumer (DTC) loans - often exceed "cost of attendance" and may be fully dischargeable.

Bar study loans - typically dischargeable under In re Campbell / McDaniel reasoning.

Mixed-use loans - fact-specific; the burden is on the creditor to prove qualified-loan status.

See private student loan dischargeability.

Florida Federal Bankruptcy Data

Student loan adversary proceedings are filed within an underlying Chapter 7 or 13 case. The Florida consumer bankruptcy volume below shows the size of the pool where a 523(a)(8) complaint could be brought.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 46,008 consumer bankruptcy cases from Florida's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 724,38994.2%5.1%

Chapter 1321,61951.3%48.6%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Florida Chapter 13 and Student Loans

In Chapter 13, student loans are generally paid pro-rata with other unsecured debt through the plan under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(1). The debtor may still file an adversary proceeding for discharge on undue hardship grounds, either during the case or after plan completion.

Practical advantages of the Chapter 13 path in Florida:

The automatic stay halts collection during the 3-5 year plan.

Accrued interest may be reduced through plan treatment.

A post-plan discharge adversary may succeed where a pre-plan one would not, because a completed plan is strong good-faith evidence.

See Chapter 13 and student loans.

Attorney Fees for Florida Adversary Proceedings

Student loan adversary proceedings carry fees in addition to the base Chapter 7 or 13 attorney fee. Typical Florida range: $2,000-$6,000 depending on case complexity and whether the loan holder contests discharge.

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 329(b), the bankruptcy court may review any attorney fee paid "in connection with" the case, including adversary-proceeding fees. Any fee paid for student loan litigation must be disclosed under Rule 2016(b) and is subject to the reasonableness standard. See Section 329 fee disgorgement overview.

Foundational Caselaw

The cases below define the doctrine on this site:

Brunner v. New York State Higher Educ. Servs. Corp., 831 F.2d 395 (2d Cir. 1987) - origin of the three-prong undue-hardship test (per curiam).

McDaniel v. Navient Solutions, LLC, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020) - private student loans outside Section 523(a)(8) scope.

Rosenberg v. New York State Higher Educ. Servs. Corp., 610 B.R. 454 (S.D.N.Y. 2020) - seminal post-Brunner critique; catalyst for the 2022 DOJ attestation guidance.

Long v. Educational Credit Mgmt. Corp., 322 F.3d 549 (8th Cir. 2003) - totality-of-circumstances alternative.

## Student Loan Bankruptcy in Georgia [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR
Source: https://bankruptcystudentloans.org/states/georgia.html

← bankruptcystudentloans.org home

Student Loan Bankruptcy in Georgia [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Georgia residents.

Student Loan Discharge in Georgia

Georgia sits in the Eleventh Circuit, which applies the Brunner three-prong test. Each prong must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence in an adversary proceeding.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). To discharge them, the debtor must file an adversary proceeding within the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the test applied in the Eleventh Circuit.

The Eleventh Circuit Brunner Standard

Applies Brunner. In re Cox, 338 F.3d 1238 (11th Cir. 2003). The Hemar Ins. Corp. v. Cox line has been influential on the second prong.

Brunner (where it applies) requires the debtor to prove:

Minimal standard of living. That the debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and dependents if forced to repay the loans.

Persistence. That additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. That the debtor has made good faith efforts to repay the loans (including IDR/IBR enrollment, forbearances attempted, and payment history).

See the full Brunner test explanation.

DOJ/DOE Attestation Process (Nov 2022)

In November 2022, the Department of Justice and Department of Education issued joint guidance that streamlines student loan discharge for federal loans. The guidance applies in every federal court, including those in Georgia, and has materially increased discharge success rates.

Under the attestation process:

The debtor completes a standardized DOJ attestation form documenting income, expenses, and repayment history.

The DOJ reviews the attestation and, in most cases, supports discharge rather than contesting.

The underlying Brunner/totality analysis is applied, but with DOJ alignment.

The U.S. Trustee in Georgia processes adversary proceedings consistent with this guidance. See adversary proceeding mechanics.

Georgia Disability and TPD Discharge

GA HOPE-related assistance; federal TPD for disability. For Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) or Social Security Supplemental Security Income (SSI) recipients, federal loans qualify for Total and Permanent Disability (TPD) discharge without bankruptcy. VA determination - Service-connected disability rated 100% or Individual Unemployability.

SSA determination - SSDI or SSI approval with a 5-7 year scheduled review flag.

Physician certification - M.D. or D.O. certifies that a medical impairment prevents substantial gainful activity.

TPD is the first path to check for any Georgia debtor with a disability. Bankruptcy discharge is the fallback when TPD is unavailable or for private loans.

Before filing an adversary proceeding, most courts in the Eleventh Circuit require the debtor to show they have attempted income-driven repayment (IDR). Below-national median areas have low IDR calculation bases.

Federal IDR plans available:

SAVE (formerly REPAYE) - 5-10% of discretionary income; lowest monthly payments for most debtors.

PAYE - 10% of discretionary income; 20-year forgiveness.

IBR - 10-15% of discretionary income; 20-25 year forgiveness.

ICR - 20% of discretionary income or 12-year standard, whichever less.

A Georgia debtor at poverty-line income typically has a $0 monthly IDR payment under SAVE. This is important for the Brunner good-faith prong: you must show you tried IDR, not that IDR was impossible.

Navient, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020), and similar reasoning in other circuits, a "qualified education loan" under 523(a)(8)(B) requires the funds to have been used solely for qualified educational expenses. Loans for living expenses, test preparation, or bar study may be dischargeable without proving undue hardship.

For Georgia debtors with private loans:

Direct-to-consumer (DTC) loans - often exceed "cost of attendance" and may be fully dischargeable.

Bar study loans - typically dischargeable under In re Campbell / McDaniel reasoning.

Mixed-use loans - fact-specific; the burden is on the creditor to prove qualified-loan status.

See private student loan dischargeability.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 1,240 consumer bankruptcy cases from Georgia's federal bankruptcy courts.

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

## Student Loan Bankruptcy in Hawaii [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR
Source: https://bankruptcystudentloans.org/states/hawaii.html

← bankruptcystudentloans.org home

Student Loan Bankruptcy in Hawaii [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Hawaii residents.

Student Loan Discharge in Hawaii

Hawaii sits in the 9th Circuit, which applies Brunner with the Pena gloss. Partial discharges are available, and the DOJ/DOE November 2022 guidance is well-integrated in 9th Circuit practice.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). To discharge them, the debtor must file an adversary proceeding within the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the test applied in the Ninth Circuit.

The Ninth Circuit Brunner Standard

Applies Brunner. In re Pena, 155 F.3d 1108 (9th Cir. 1998). Allows partial discharge and considers payment-history attempts favorably under DOJ/DOE guidance.

Brunner (where it applies) requires the debtor to prove:

Minimal standard of living. That the debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and dependents if forced to repay the loans.

Persistence. That additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. That the debtor has made good faith efforts to repay the loans (including IDR/IBR enrollment, forbearances attempted, and payment history).

See the full Brunner test explanation.

In November 2022, the Department of Justice and Department of Education issued joint guidance that streamlines student loan discharge for federal loans. The guidance applies in every federal court, including those in Hawaii, and has materially increased discharge success rates.

Under the attestation process:

The debtor completes a standardized DOJ attestation form documenting income, expenses, and repayment history.

The DOJ reviews the attestation and, in most cases, supports discharge rather than contesting.

The underlying Brunner/totality analysis is applied, but with DOJ alignment.

The U.S. Trustee in Hawaii processes adversary proceedings consistent with this guidance. See adversary proceeding mechanics.

HI Health Service Corps; federal TPD. For Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) or Social Security Supplemental Security Income (SSI) recipients, federal loans qualify for Total and Permanent Disability (TPD) discharge without bankruptcy. TPD is administrative - no adversary proceeding needed - and applies to federal Direct, FFEL, and Perkins loans.

Physician certification - M.D. or D.O. certifies that a medical impairment prevents substantial gainful activity.

TPD is the first path to check for any Hawaii debtor with a disability. Bankruptcy discharge is the fallback when TPD is unavailable or for private loans.

Before filing an adversary proceeding, most courts in the Ninth Circuit require the debtor to show they have attempted income-driven repayment (IDR). Hawaii COL adjustment is among the highest in the federal IDR modeling.

Federal IDR plans available:

SAVE (formerly REPAYE) - 5-10% of discretionary income; lowest monthly payments for most debtors.

PAYE - 10% of discretionary income; 20-year forgiveness.

IBR - 10-15% of discretionary income; 20-25 year forgiveness.

ICR - 20% of discretionary income or 12-year standard, whichever less.

A Hawaii debtor at poverty-line income typically has a $0 monthly IDR payment under SAVE. This is important for the Brunner good-faith prong: you must show you tried IDR, not that IDR was impossible.

Navient, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020), and similar reasoning in other circuits, a "qualified education loan" under 523(a)(8)(B) requires the funds to have been used solely for qualified educational expenses. Bar study loans - typically dischargeable under In re Campbell / McDaniel reasoning.

Mixed-use loans - fact-specific; the burden is on the creditor to prove qualified-loan status.

See private student loan dischargeability.

In Chapter 13, student loans are generally paid pro-rata with other unsecured debt through the plan under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(1). The debtor may still file an adversary proceeding for discharge on undue hardship grounds, either during the case or after plan completion.

Practical advantages of the Chapter 13 path in Hawaii:

The automatic stay halts collection during the 3-5 year plan.

Accrued interest may be reduced through plan treatment.

A post-plan discharge adversary may succeed where a pre-plan one would not, because a completed plan is strong good-faith evidence.

See Chapter 13 and student loans.

Attorney Fees for Hawaii Adversary Proceedings

Student loan adversary proceedings carry fees in addition to the base Chapter 7 or 13 attorney fee. Typical Hawaii range: $2,000-$6,000 depending on case complexity and whether the loan holder contests discharge.

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 329(b), the bankruptcy court may review any attorney fee paid "in connection with" the case, including adversary-proceeding fees. Any fee paid for student loan litigation must be disclosed under Rule 2016(b) and is subject to the reasonableness standard. See Section 329 fee disgorgement overview.

## Student Loan Bankruptcy in Illinois [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR
Source: https://bankruptcystudentloans.org/states/illinois.html

← bankruptcystudentloans.org home

Student Loan Bankruptcy in Illinois [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Illinois residents.

Student Loan Discharge in Illinois

Illinois sits in the Seventh Circuit, which applies the Brunner three-prong test. Each prong must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence in an adversary proceeding.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). To discharge them, the debtor must file an adversary proceeding within the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the test applied in the Seventh Circuit.

The Seventh Circuit Brunner Standard

Applies Brunner. In re Roberson, 999 F.2d 1132 (7th Cir. 1993). Partial discharges available under In re Saxman-style reasoning.

Brunner (where it applies) requires the debtor to prove:

Minimal standard of living. That the debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and dependents if forced to repay the loans.

Persistence. That additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. That the debtor has made good faith efforts to repay the loans (including IDR/IBR enrollment, forbearances attempted, and payment history).

PAYE - 10% of discretionary income; 20-year forgiveness.

IBR - 10-15% of discretionary income; 20-25 year forgiveness.

ICR - 20% of discretionary income or 12-year standard, whichever less.

A Illinois debtor at poverty-line income typically has a $0 monthly IDR payment under SAVE. This is important for the Brunner good-faith prong: you must show you tried IDR, not that IDR was impossible.

Private Student Loans in Illinois

Private student loans are treated differently. Under the 10th Circuit's McDaniel v. Navient, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020), and similar reasoning in other circuits, a "qualified education loan" under 523(a)(8)(B) requires the funds to have been used solely for qualified educational expenses. Loans for living expenses, test preparation, or bar study may be dischargeable without proving undue hardship.

For Illinois debtors with private loans:

Direct-to-consumer (DTC) loans - often exceed "cost of attendance" and may be fully dischargeable.

Bar study loans - typically dischargeable under In re Campbell / McDaniel reasoning.

Mixed-use loans - fact-specific; the burden is on the creditor to prove qualified-loan status.

See private student loan dischargeability.

Illinois Federal Bankruptcy Data

Student loan adversary proceedings are filed within an underlying Chapter 7 or 13 case. The Illinois consumer bankruptcy volume below shows the size of the pool where a 523(a)(8) complaint could be brought.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 9,898 consumer bankruptcy cases from Illinois's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 76,72999.5%0.4%

Chapter 133,16945.9%53.7%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Illinois Chapter 13 and Student Loans

In Chapter 13, student loans are generally paid pro-rata with other unsecured debt through the plan under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(1). The debtor may still file an adversary proceeding for discharge on undue hardship grounds, either during the case or after plan completion.

Practical advantages of the Chapter 13 path in Illinois:

The automatic stay halts collection during the 3-5 year plan.

Accrued interest may be reduced through plan treatment.

A post-plan discharge adversary may succeed where a pre-plan one would not, because a completed plan is strong good-faith evidence.

See Chapter 13 and student loans.

Attorney Fees for Illinois Adversary Proceedings

Student loan adversary proceedings carry fees in addition to the base Chapter 7 or 13 attorney fee. Typical Illinois range: $2,000-$6,000 depending on case complexity and whether the loan holder contests discharge.

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 329(b), the bankruptcy court may review any attorney fee paid "in connection with" the case, including adversary-proceeding fees. Any fee paid for student loan litigation must be disclosed under Rule 2016(b) and is subject to the reasonableness standard. See Section 329 fee disgorgement overview.

Foundational Caselaw

The cases below define the doctrine on this site:

Brunner v. New York State Higher Educ. Servs. Corp., 831 F.2d 395 (2d Cir. 1987) - origin of the three-prong undue-hardship test (per curiam).

McDaniel v. Navient Solutions, LLC, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020) - private student loans outside Section 523(a)(8) scope.

Rosenberg v. New York State Higher Educ. Servs. Corp., 610 B.R. 454 (S.D.N.Y. 2020) - seminal post-Brunner critique; catalyst for the 2022 DOJ attestation guidance.

Long v. Educational Credit Mgmt. Corp., 322 F.3d 549 (8th Cir. 2003) - totality-of-circumstances alternative.

## Student Loan Bankruptcy in Indiana [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR
Source: https://bankruptcystudentloans.org/states/indiana.html

← bankruptcystudentloans.org home

Student Loan Bankruptcy in Indiana [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Indiana residents.

Student Loan Discharge in Indiana

Indiana sits in the Seventh Circuit, which applies the Brunner three-prong test. Each prong must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence in an adversary proceeding.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). To discharge them, the debtor must file an adversary proceeding within the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the test applied in the Seventh Circuit.

The Seventh Circuit Brunner Standard

Applies Brunner. In re Roberson, 999 F.2d 1132 (7th Cir. 1993). Partial discharges available under In re Saxman-style reasoning.

Brunner (where it applies) requires the debtor to prove:

Minimal standard of living. That the debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and dependents if forced to repay the loans.

Persistence. That additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. That the debtor has made good faith efforts to repay the loans (including IDR/IBR enrollment, forbearances attempted, and payment history).

See the full Brunner test explanation.

DOJ/DOE Attestation Process (Nov 2022)

In November 2022, the Department of Justice and Department of Education issued joint guidance that streamlines student loan discharge for federal loans. The guidance applies in every federal court, including those in Indiana, and has materially increased discharge success rates.

Under the attestation process:

The debtor completes a standardized DOJ attestation form documenting income, expenses, and repayment history.

The DOJ reviews the attestation and, in most cases, supports discharge rather than contesting.

The underlying Brunner/totality analysis is applied, but with DOJ alignment.

The U.S. Trustee in Indiana processes adversary proceedings consistent with this guidance. See adversary proceeding mechanics.

Indiana Disability and TPD Discharge

IN Primary Care Physician Loan Repayment; federal TPD. For Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) or Social Security Supplemental Security Income (SSI) recipients, federal loans qualify for Total and Permanent Disability (TPD) discharge without bankruptcy. TPD is administrative - no adversary proceeding needed - and applies to federal Direct, FFEL, and Perkins loans.

Three TPD qualification paths:

VA determination - Service-connected disability rated 100% or Individual Unemployability.

SSA determination - SSDI or SSI approval with a 5-7 year scheduled review flag.

Physician certification - M.D. or D.O. certifies that a medical impairment prevents substantial gainful activity.

TPD is the first path to check for any Indiana debtor with a disability. Bankruptcy discharge is the fallback when TPD is unavailable or for private loans.

Indiana Income-Driven Repayment Baseline

Before filing an adversary proceeding, most courts in the Seventh Circuit require the debtor to show they have attempted income-driven repayment (IDR). Standard federal IDR; below-average IDR payment for most filers.

Federal IDR plans available:

SAVE (formerly REPAYE) - 5-10% of discretionary income; lowest monthly payments for most debtors.

PAYE - 10% of discretionary income; 20-year forgiveness.

IBR - 10-15% of discretionary income; 20-25 year forgiveness.

ICR - 20% of discretionary income or 12-year standard, whichever less.

A Indiana debtor at poverty-line income typically has a $0 monthly IDR payment under SAVE. This is important for the Brunner good-faith prong: you must show you tried IDR, not that IDR was impossible.

Private Student Loans in Indiana

Private student loans are treated differently. Under the 10th Circuit's McDaniel v. Navient, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020), and similar reasoning in other circuits, a "qualified education loan" under 523(a)(8)(B) requires the funds to have been used solely for qualified educational expenses. Loans for living expenses, test preparation, or bar study may be dischargeable without proving undue hardship.

For Indiana debtors with private loans:

Direct-to-consumer (DTC) loans - often exceed "cost of attendance" and may be fully dischargeable.

Bar study loans - typically dischargeable under In re Campbell / McDaniel reasoning.

Mixed-use loans - fact-specific; the burden is on the creditor to prove qualified-loan status.

See private student loan dischargeability.

Indiana Federal Bankruptcy Data

Student loan adversary proceedings are filed within an underlying Chapter 7 or 13 case. The Indiana consumer bankruptcy volume below shows the size of the pool where a 523(a)(8) complaint could be brought.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 3,325 consumer bankruptcy cases from Indiana's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 779297.5%2.0%

Chapter 132,53369.8%29.5%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Indiana Chapter 13 and Student Loans

In Chapter 13, student loans are generally paid pro-rata with other unsecured debt through the plan under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(1). The debtor may still file an adversary proceeding for discharge on undue hardship grounds, either during the case or after plan completion.

Practical advantages of the Chapter 13 path in Indiana:

The automatic stay halts collection during the 3-5 year plan.

Accrued interest may be reduced through plan treatment.

A post-plan discharge adversary may succeed where a pre-plan one would not, because a completed plan is strong good-faith evidence.

See Chapter 13 and student loans.

Attorney Fees for Indiana Adversary Proceedings

Student loan adversary proceedings carry fees in addition to the base Chapter 7 or 13 attorney fee. Typical Indiana range: $2,000-$6,000 depending on case complexity and whether the loan holder contests discharge.

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 329(b), the bankruptcy court may review any attorney fee paid "in connection with" the case, including adversary-proceeding fees. Any fee paid for student loan litigation must be disclosed under Rule 2016(b) and is subject to the reasonableness standard. See Section 329 fee disgorgement overview.

## Student Loan Bankruptcy in Iowa [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR
Source: https://bankruptcystudentloans.org/states/iowa.html

← bankruptcystudentloans.org home

Student Loan Bankruptcy in Iowa [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Iowa residents.

Student Loan Discharge in Iowa

Iowa sits in the 8th Circuit, which does NOT use the rigid Brunner test. Instead, the 8th Circuit applies a totality-of-the-circumstances test that is generally considered more favorable to debtors seeking student loan discharge. Long v. ECMC, 322 F.3d 549 (8th Cir. 2003), is the controlling authority.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). To discharge them, the debtor must file an adversary proceeding within the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the test applied in the Eighth Circuit.

The Eighth Circuit Brunner Standard

Does NOT apply Brunner. Uses totality-of-the-circumstances test. Long v. ECMC, 322 F.3d 549 (8th Cir. 2003); Educational Credit Mgmt. Corp. v. Jesperson, 571 F.3d 775 (8th Cir. 2009). Significantly more debtor-friendly in theory.

Brunner (where it applies) requires the debtor to prove:

Minimal standard of living. That the debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and dependents if forced to repay the loans.

Persistence. That additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. That the debtor has made good faith efforts to repay the loans (including IDR/IBR enrollment, forbearances attempted, and payment history).

See the full Brunner test explanation.

The debtor completes a standardized DOJ attestation form documenting income, expenses, and repayment history.

The DOJ reviews the attestation and, in most cases, supports discharge rather than contesting.

The underlying Brunner/totality analysis is applied, but with DOJ alignment.

The U.S. Trustee in Iowa processes adversary proceedings consistent with this guidance. See adversary proceeding mechanics.

Before filing an adversary proceeding, most courts in the Eighth Circuit require the debtor to show they have attempted income-driven repayment (IDR). Rural-service forgiveness often more lucrative than discharge for IA debtors.

Federal IDR plans available:

SAVE (formerly REPAYE) - 5-10% of discretionary income; lowest monthly payments for most debtors.

PAYE - 10% of discretionary income; 20-year forgiveness.

IBR - 10-15% of discretionary income; 20-25 year forgiveness.

ICR - 20% of discretionary income or 12-year standard, whichever less.

A Iowa debtor at poverty-line income typically has a $0 monthly IDR payment under SAVE. This is important for the Brunner good-faith prong: you must show you tried IDR, not that IDR was impossible.

Mixed-use loans - fact-specific; the burden is on the creditor to prove qualified-loan status.

See private student loan dischargeability.

Practical advantages of the Chapter 13 path in Iowa:

The automatic stay halts collection during the 3-5 year plan.

Accrued interest may be reduced through plan treatment.

A post-plan discharge adversary may succeed where a pre-plan one would not, because a completed plan is strong good-faith evidence.

See Chapter 13 and student loans.

## Student Loan Bankruptcy in Kansas [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR
Source: https://bankruptcystudentloans.org/states/kansas.html

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Kansas residents.

Kansas sits in the Tenth Circuit, which applies the Brunner three-prong test. Each prong must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence in an adversary proceeding.

The Tenth Circuit Brunner Standard

Applies Brunner. In re Woodcock, 45 F.3d 363 (10th Cir. 1995). Recent panels have loosened the good-faith prong; see McDaniel v. Navient (2020) on tuition-vs-educational distinction.

Brunner (where it applies) requires the debtor to prove:

Minimal standard of living. That the debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and dependents if forced to repay the loans.

Persistence. That additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

## Student Loan Bankruptcy in Kentucky [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR
Source: https://bankruptcystudentloans.org/states/kentucky.html

← bankruptcystudentloans.org home

Student Loan Bankruptcy in Kentucky [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Kentucky residents.

Student Loan Discharge in Kentucky

Kentucky sits in the Sixth Circuit, which applies the Brunner three-prong test. Each prong must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence in an adversary proceeding.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). To discharge them, the debtor must file an adversary proceeding within the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the test applied in the Sixth Circuit.

The Sixth Circuit Brunner Standard

Applies Brunner. In re Oyler, 397 F.3d 382 (6th Cir. 2005). Good-faith considered based on repayment history and lifestyle choices.

Brunner (where it applies) requires the debtor to prove:

Minimal standard of living. That the debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and dependents if forced to repay the loans.

Persistence. That additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. That the debtor has made good faith efforts to repay the loans (including IDR/IBR enrollment, forbearances attempted, and payment history).

The DOJ reviews the attestation and, in most cases, supports discharge rather than contesting.

The underlying Brunner/totality analysis is applied, but with DOJ alignment.

The U.S. Trustee in Kentucky processes adversary proceedings consistent with this guidance. See adversary proceeding mechanics.

TPD is the first path to check for any Kentucky debtor with a disability. Bankruptcy discharge is the fallback when TPD is unavailable or for private loans.

Kentucky Income-Driven Repayment Baseline

Before filing an adversary proceeding, most courts in the Sixth Circuit require the debtor to show they have attempted income-driven repayment (IDR). Low median income; SAVE plan covers many KY debtors at $0/month.

Federal IDR plans available:

SAVE (formerly REPAYE) - 5-10% of discretionary income; lowest monthly payments for most debtors.

PAYE - 10% of discretionary income; 20-year forgiveness.

IBR - 10-15% of discretionary income; 20-25 year forgiveness.

ICR - 20% of discretionary income or 12-year standard, whichever less.

A Kentucky debtor at poverty-line income typically has a $0 monthly IDR payment under SAVE. This is important for the Brunner good-faith prong: you must show you tried IDR, not that IDR was impossible.

Private Student Loans in Kentucky

Private student loans are treated differently. Under the 10th Circuit's McDaniel v. Navient, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020), and similar reasoning in other circuits, a "qualified education loan" under 523(a)(8)(B) requires the funds to have been used solely for qualified educational expenses. Loans for living expenses, test preparation, or bar study may be dischargeable without proving undue hardship.

For Kentucky debtors with private loans:

Direct-to-consumer (DTC) loans - often exceed "cost of attendance" and may be fully dischargeable.

Bar study loans - typically dischargeable under In re Campbell / McDaniel reasoning.

Mixed-use loans - fact-specific; the burden is on the creditor to prove qualified-loan status.

See private student loan dischargeability.

Kentucky Federal Bankruptcy Data

Student loan adversary proceedings are filed within an underlying Chapter 7 or 13 case. The Kentucky consumer bankruptcy volume below shows the size of the pool where a 523(a)(8) complaint could be brought.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 1,692 consumer bankruptcy cases from Kentucky's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 731897.5%1.7%

Chapter 131,37472.1%27.0%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Kentucky Chapter 13 and Student Loans

In Chapter 13, student loans are generally paid pro-rata with other unsecured debt through the plan under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(1). The debtor may still file an adversary proceeding for discharge on undue hardship grounds, either during the case or after plan completion.

Practical advantages of the Chapter 13 path in Kentucky:

The automatic stay halts collection during the 3-5 year plan.

Accrued interest may be reduced through plan treatment.

A post-plan discharge adversary may succeed where a pre-plan one would not, because a completed plan is strong good-faith evidence.

See Chapter 13 and student loans.

Attorney Fees for Kentucky Adversary Proceedings

Student loan adversary proceedings carry fees in addition to the base Chapter 7 or 13 attorney fee. Typical Kentucky range: $2,000-$6,000 depending on case complexity and whether the loan holder contests discharge.

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 329(b), the bankruptcy court may review any attorney fee paid "in connection with" the case, including adversary-proceeding fees. Any fee paid for student loan litigation must be disclosed under Rule 2016(b) and is subject to the reasonableness standard. See Section 329 fee disgorgement overview.

Foundational Caselaw

The cases below define the doctrine on this site:

Brunner v. New York State Higher Educ. Servs. Corp., 831 F.2d 395 (2d Cir. 1987) - origin of the three-prong undue-hardship test (per curiam).

McDaniel v. Navient Solutions, LLC, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020) - private student loans outside Section 523(a)(8) scope.

Rosenberg v. New York State Higher Educ. Servs. Corp., 610 B.R. 454 (S.D.N.Y. 2020) - seminal post-Brunner critique; catalyst for the 2022 DOJ attestation guidance.

Long v. Educational Credit Mgmt. Corp., 322 F.3d 549 (8th Cir. 2003) - totality-of-circumstances alternative.

## Student Loan Bankruptcy in Louisiana [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR
Source: https://bankruptcystudentloans.org/states/louisiana.html

← bankruptcystudentloans.org home

Student Loan Bankruptcy in Louisiana [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Louisiana residents.

Student Loan Discharge in Louisiana

Louisiana sits in the Fifth Circuit, which applies the Brunner three-prong test. Each prong must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence in an adversary proceeding.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). To discharge them, the debtor must file an adversary proceeding within the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the test applied in the Fifth Circuit.

The Fifth Circuit Brunner Standard

Applies Brunner. In re Gerhardt, 348 F.3d 89 (5th Cir. 2003). Historically strict; the 2019 Thomas decision narrowed "minimal standard of living" but also reaffirmed Brunner.

Brunner (where it applies) requires the debtor to prove:

Minimal standard of living. That the debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and dependents if forced to repay the loans.

Persistence. That additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. That the debtor has made good faith efforts to repay the loans (including IDR/IBR enrollment, forbearances attempted, and payment history).

See the full Brunner test explanation.

DOJ/DOE Attestation Process (Nov 2022)

In November 2022, the Department of Justice and Department of Education issued joint guidance that streamlines student loan discharge for federal loans. The guidance applies in every federal court, including those in Louisiana, and has materially increased discharge success rates.

Under the attestation process:

The debtor completes a standardized DOJ attestation form documenting income, expenses, and repayment history.

The DOJ reviews the attestation and, in most cases, supports discharge rather than contesting.

The underlying Brunner/totality analysis is applied, but with DOJ alignment.

The U.S. Trustee in Louisiana processes adversary proceedings consistent with this guidance. See adversary proceeding mechanics.

Louisiana Disability and TPD Discharge

Limited state programs; federal TPD primary path. For Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) or Social Security Supplemental Security Income (SSI) recipients, federal loans qualify for Total and Permanent Disability (TPD) discharge without bankruptcy. TPD is administrative - no adversary proceeding needed - and applies to federal Direct, FFEL, and Perkins loans.

Three TPD qualification paths:

VA determination - Service-connected disability rated 100% or Individual Unemployability.

SSA determination - SSDI or SSI approval with a 5-7 year scheduled review flag.

Physician certification - M.D. or D.O. certifies that a medical impairment prevents substantial gainful activity.

TPD is the first path to check for any Louisiana debtor with a disability. Bankruptcy discharge is the fallback when TPD is unavailable or for private loans.

Louisiana Income-Driven Repayment Baseline

Before filing an adversary proceeding, most courts in the Fifth Circuit require the debtor to show they have attempted income-driven repayment (IDR). Louisiana has among the highest Chapter 13 dismissal rates; student loan hardship compounds that.

Federal IDR plans available:

SAVE (formerly REPAYE) - 5-10% of discretionary income; lowest monthly payments for most debtors.

PAYE - 10% of discretionary income; 20-year forgiveness.

IBR - 10-15% of discretionary income; 20-25 year forgiveness.

ICR - 20% of discretionary income or 12-year standard, whichever less.

A Louisiana debtor at poverty-line income typically has a $0 monthly IDR payment under SAVE. This is important for the Brunner good-faith prong: you must show you tried IDR, not that IDR was impossible.

Private Student Loans in Louisiana

Private student loans are treated differently. Under the 10th Circuit's McDaniel v. Navient, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020), and similar reasoning in other circuits, a "qualified education loan" under 523(a)(8)(B) requires the funds to have been used solely for qualified educational expenses. Loans for living expenses, test preparation, or bar study may be dischargeable without proving undue hardship.

For Louisiana debtors with private loans:

Direct-to-consumer (DTC) loans - often exceed "cost of attendance" and may be fully dischargeable.

Bar study loans - typically dischargeable under In re Campbell / McDaniel reasoning.

Mixed-use loans - fact-specific; the burden is on the creditor to prove qualified-loan status.

See private student loan dischargeability.

Louisiana Chapter 13 and Student Loans

In Chapter 13, student loans are generally paid pro-rata with other unsecured debt through the plan under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(1). The debtor may still file an adversary proceeding for discharge on undue hardship grounds, either during the case or after plan completion.

Practical advantages of the Chapter 13 path in Louisiana:

The automatic stay halts collection during the 3-5 year plan.

Accrued interest may be reduced through plan treatment.

A post-plan discharge adversary may succeed where a pre-plan one would not, because a completed plan is strong good-faith evidence.

See Chapter 13 and student loans.

Attorney Fees for Louisiana Adversary Proceedings

Student loan adversary proceedings carry fees in addition to the base Chapter 7 or 13 attorney fee. Typical Louisiana range: $2,000-$6,000 depending on case complexity and whether the loan holder contests discharge.

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 329(b), the bankruptcy court may review any attorney fee paid "in connection with" the case, including adversary-proceeding fees. Any fee paid for student loan litigation must be disclosed under Rule 2016(b) and is subject to the reasonableness standard. See Section 329 fee disgorgement overview.

## Student Loan Bankruptcy in Maine [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR
Source: https://bankruptcystudentloans.org/states/maine.html

← bankruptcystudentloans.org home

Student Loan Bankruptcy in Maine [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Maine residents.

Student Loan Discharge in Maine

Maine sits in the 1st Circuit, which blends Brunner with totality-of-the-circumstances flexibility. Partial discharges and equitable considerations are more accessible than in strict-Brunner circuits.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). To discharge them, the debtor must file an adversary proceeding within the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the test applied in the First Circuit.

The First Circuit Brunner Standard

Uses a blend of Brunner and totality-of-circumstances. Bronsdon v. Educ. Credit Mgmt. Corp., 435 B.R. 791 (1st Cir. BAP 2010); In re Nash, 446 F.3d 188 (1st Cir. 2006) allows flexibility on the "additional circumstances" prong.

Brunner (where it applies) requires the debtor to prove:

Minimal standard of living. That the debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and dependents if forced to repay the loans.

Persistence. That additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. That the debtor has made good faith efforts to repay the loans (including IDR/IBR enrollment, forbearances attempted, and payment history).

Before filing an adversary proceeding, most courts in the First Circuit require the debtor to show they have attempted income-driven repayment (IDR). ME has active federal TPD outreach through state legal aid.

Federal IDR plans available:

SAVE (formerly REPAYE) - 5-10% of discretionary income; lowest monthly payments for most debtors.

PAYE - 10% of discretionary income; 20-year forgiveness.

IBR - 10-15% of discretionary income; 20-25 year forgiveness.

## Student Loan Bankruptcy in Maryland [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR
Source: https://bankruptcystudentloans.org/states/maryland.html

← bankruptcystudentloans.org home

Student Loan Bankruptcy in Maryland [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Maryland residents.

Applies Brunner. In re Frushour, 433 F.3d 393 (4th Cir. 2005). Strict good-faith inquiry; debtors expected to document IBR/IDR attempts.

Brunner (where it applies) requires the debtor to prove:

Minimal standard of living. That the debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and dependents if forced to repay the loans.

Chapter 71,29098.3%0.9%

Chapter 136659.1%40.9%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Massachusetts Chapter 13 and Student Loans

In Chapter 13, student loans are generally paid pro-rata with other unsecured debt through the plan under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(1). The debtor may still file an adversary proceeding for discharge on undue hardship grounds, either during the case or after plan completion.

Practical advantages of the Chapter 13 path in Massachusetts:

The automatic stay halts collection during the 3-5 year plan.

Accrued interest may be reduced through plan treatment.

A post-plan discharge adversary may succeed where a pre-plan one would not, because a completed plan is strong good-faith evidence.

See Chapter 13 and student loans.

Attorney Fees for Massachusetts Adversary Proceedings

Student loan adversary proceedings carry fees in addition to the base Chapter 7 or 13 attorney fee. Typical Massachusetts range: $2,000-$6,000 depending on case complexity and whether the loan holder contests discharge.

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 329(b), the bankruptcy court may review any attorney fee paid "in connection with" the case, including adversary-proceeding fees. Any fee paid for student loan litigation must be disclosed under Rule 2016(b) and is subject to the reasonableness standard. See Section 329 fee disgorgement overview.

Rosenberg v. New York State Higher Educ. Servs. Corp., 610 B.R. 454 (S.D.N.Y. 2020) - seminal post-Brunner critique; catalyst for the 2022 DOJ attestation guidance.

Long v. Educational Credit Mgmt. Corp., 322 F.3d 549 (8th Cir. 2003) - totality-of-circumstances alternative.

## Student Loan Bankruptcy in Michigan [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR
Source: https://bankruptcystudentloans.org/states/michigan.html

← bankruptcystudentloans.org home

Student Loan Bankruptcy in Michigan [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Michigan residents.

Student Loan Discharge in Michigan

Michigan sits in the Sixth Circuit, which applies the Brunner three-prong test. Each prong must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence in an adversary proceeding.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). To discharge them, the debtor must file an adversary proceeding within the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the test applied in the Sixth Circuit.

The Sixth Circuit Brunner Standard

Applies Brunner. In re Oyler, 397 F.3d 382 (6th Cir. 2005). Good-faith considered based on repayment history and lifestyle choices.

Brunner (where it applies) requires the debtor to prove:

Minimal standard of living. That the debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and dependents if forced to repay the loans.

Persistence. That additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. That the debtor has made good faith efforts to repay the loans (including IDR/IBR enrollment, forbearances attempted, and payment history).

See the full Brunner test explanation.

DOJ/DOE Attestation Process (Nov 2022)

In November 2022, the Department of Justice and Department of Education issued joint guidance that streamlines student loan discharge for federal loans. The guidance applies in every federal court, including those in Michigan, and has materially increased discharge success rates.

Under the attestation process:

The debtor completes a standardized DOJ attestation form documenting income, expenses, and repayment history.

The DOJ reviews the attestation and, in most cases, supports discharge rather than contesting.

The underlying Brunner/totality analysis is applied, but with DOJ alignment.

The U.S. Trustee in Michigan processes adversary proceedings consistent with this guidance. See adversary proceeding mechanics.

Michigan Disability and TPD Discharge

MI Dental Scholarship, MI Nurse Educator; federal TPD. For Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) or Social Security Supplemental Security Income (SSI) recipients, federal loans qualify for Total and Permanent Disability (TPD) discharge without bankruptcy. TPD is administrative - no adversary proceeding needed - and applies to federal Direct, FFEL, and Perkins loans.

Three TPD qualification paths:

VA determination - Service-connected disability rated 100% or Individual Unemployability.

SSA determination - SSDI or SSI approval with a 5-7 year scheduled review flag.

Physician certification - M.D. or D.O. certifies that a medical impairment prevents substantial gainful activity.

TPD is the first path to check for any Michigan debtor with a disability. Bankruptcy discharge is the fallback when TPD is unavailable or for private loans.

Michigan Income-Driven Repayment Baseline

Before filing an adversary proceeding, most courts in the Sixth Circuit require the debtor to show they have attempted income-driven repayment (IDR). Detroit metro COL modeling can reduce IDR payments.

Federal IDR plans available:

SAVE (formerly REPAYE) - 5-10% of discretionary income; lowest monthly payments for most debtors.

PAYE - 10% of discretionary income; 20-year forgiveness.

IBR - 10-15% of discretionary income; 20-25 year forgiveness.

ICR - 20% of discretionary income or 12-year standard, whichever less.

A Michigan debtor at poverty-line income typically has a $0 monthly IDR payment under SAVE. This is important for the Brunner good-faith prong: you must show you tried IDR, not that IDR was impossible.

Private Student Loans in Michigan

Private student loans are treated differently. Under the 10th Circuit's McDaniel v. Navient, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020), and similar reasoning in other circuits, a "qualified education loan" under 523(a)(8)(B) requires the funds to have been used solely for qualified educational expenses. Loans for living expenses, test preparation, or bar study may be dischargeable without proving undue hardship.

For Michigan debtors with private loans:

Direct-to-consumer (DTC) loans - often exceed "cost of attendance" and may be fully dischargeable.

Bar study loans - typically dischargeable under In re Campbell / McDaniel reasoning.

Mixed-use loans - fact-specific; the burden is on the creditor to prove qualified-loan status.

See private student loan dischargeability.

Michigan Federal Bankruptcy Data

Student loan adversary proceedings are filed within an underlying Chapter 7 or 13 case. The Michigan consumer bankruptcy volume below shows the size of the pool where a 523(a)(8) complaint could be brought.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 1,133 consumer bankruptcy cases from Michigan's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 7633100.0%0.0%

Chapter 1350048.3%51.0%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Michigan Chapter 13 and Student Loans

In Chapter 13, student loans are generally paid pro-rata with other unsecured debt through the plan under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(1). The debtor may still file an adversary proceeding for discharge on undue hardship grounds, either during the case or after plan completion.

Practical advantages of the Chapter 13 path in Michigan:

The automatic stay halts collection during the 3-5 year plan.

Accrued interest may be reduced through plan treatment.

A post-plan discharge adversary may succeed where a pre-plan one would not, because a completed plan is strong good-faith evidence.

See Chapter 13 and student loans.

Attorney Fees for Michigan Adversary Proceedings

Student loan adversary proceedings carry fees in addition to the base Chapter 7 or 13 attorney fee. Typical Michigan range: $2,000-$6,000 depending on case complexity and whether the loan holder contests discharge.

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 329(b), the bankruptcy court may review any attorney fee paid "in connection with" the case, including adversary-proceeding fees. Any fee paid for student loan litigation must be disclosed under Rule 2016(b) and is subject to the reasonableness standard. See Section 329 fee disgorgement overview.

## Student Loan Bankruptcy in Minnesota [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR
Source: https://bankruptcystudentloans.org/states/minnesota.html

← bankruptcystudentloans.org home

Student Loan Bankruptcy in Minnesota [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Minnesota residents.

Student Loan Discharge in Minnesota

Minnesota sits in the 8th Circuit, which does NOT use the rigid Brunner test. Instead, the 8th Circuit applies a totality-of-the-circumstances test that is generally considered more favorable to debtors seeking student loan discharge. Long v. ECMC, 322 F.3d 549 (8th Cir. 2003), is the controlling authority.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). To discharge them, the debtor must file an adversary proceeding within the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the test applied in the Eighth Circuit.

The Eighth Circuit Brunner Standard

Does NOT apply Brunner. Uses totality-of-the-circumstances test. Long v. ECMC, 322 F.3d 549 (8th Cir. 2003); Educational Credit Mgmt. Corp. v. Jesperson, 571 F.3d 775 (8th Cir. 2009). Significantly more debtor-friendly in theory.

Brunner (where it applies) requires the debtor to prove:

Minimal standard of living. That the debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and dependents if forced to repay the loans.

Persistence. That additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. That the debtor has made good faith efforts to repay the loans (including IDR/IBR enrollment, forbearances attempted, and payment history).

Any fee paid for student loan litigation must be disclosed under Rule 2016(b) and is subject to the reasonableness standard. See Section 329 fee disgorgement overview.

## Student Loan Bankruptcy in Montana [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR
Source: https://bankruptcystudentloans.org/states/montana.html

← bankruptcystudentloans.org home

Student Loan Bankruptcy in Montana [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Montana residents.

Student Loan Discharge in Montana

Montana sits in the 9th Circuit, which applies Brunner with the Pena gloss. Partial discharges are available, and the DOJ/DOE November 2022 guidance is well-integrated in 9th Circuit practice.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). To discharge them, the debtor must file an adversary proceeding within the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the test applied in the Ninth Circuit.

The Ninth Circuit Brunner Standard

Applies Brunner. In re Pena, 155 F.3d 1108 (9th Cir. 1998). Allows partial discharge and considers payment-history attempts favorably under DOJ/DOE guidance.

Brunner (where it applies) requires the debtor to prove:

Minimal standard of living. That the debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and dependents if forced to repay the loans.

Persistence. That additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. That the debtor has made good faith efforts to repay the loans (including IDR/IBR enrollment, forbearances attempted, and payment history).

See the full Brunner test explanation.

DOJ/DOE Attestation Process (Nov 2022)

In November 2022, the Department of Justice and Department of Education issued joint guidance that streamlines student loan discharge for federal loans. The guidance applies in every federal court, including those in Montana, and has materially increased discharge success rates.

Under the attestation process:

The debtor completes a standardized DOJ attestation form documenting income, expenses, and repayment history.

The DOJ reviews the attestation and, in most cases, supports discharge rather than contesting.

The underlying Brunner/totality analysis is applied, but with DOJ alignment.

The U.S. Trustee in Montana processes adversary proceedings consistent with this guidance. See adversary proceeding mechanics.

Montana Disability and TPD Discharge

MT Institutional Nursing Incentive; federal TPD. For Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) or Social Security Supplemental Security Income (SSI) recipients, federal loans qualify for Total and Permanent Disability (TPD) discharge without bankruptcy. TPD is administrative - no adversary proceeding needed - and applies to federal Direct, FFEL, and Perkins loans.

Three TPD qualification paths:

VA determination - Service-connected disability rated 100% or Individual Unemployability.

SSA determination - SSDI or SSI approval with a 5-7 year scheduled review flag.

Physician certification - M.D. or D.O. certifies that a medical impairment prevents substantial gainful activity.

TPD is the first path to check for any Montana debtor with a disability. Bankruptcy discharge is the fallback when TPD is unavailable or for private loans.

Montana Income-Driven Repayment Baseline

Before filing an adversary proceeding, most courts in the Ninth Circuit require the debtor to show they have attempted income-driven repayment (IDR). Rural service tracks offer alternative to discharge.

Federal IDR plans available:

SAVE (formerly REPAYE) - 5-10% of discretionary income; lowest monthly payments for most debtors.

PAYE - 10% of discretionary income; 20-year forgiveness.

IBR - 10-15% of discretionary income; 20-25 year forgiveness.

ICR - 20% of discretionary income or 12-year standard, whichever less.

A Montana debtor at poverty-line income typically has a $0 monthly IDR payment under SAVE. This is important for the Brunner good-faith prong: you must show you tried IDR, not that IDR was impossible.

Private Student Loans in Montana

Private student loans are treated differently. Under the 10th Circuit's McDaniel v. Navient, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020), and similar reasoning in other circuits, a "qualified education loan" under 523(a)(8)(B) requires the funds to have been used solely for qualified educational expenses. Loans for living expenses, test preparation, or bar study may be dischargeable without proving undue hardship.

For Montana debtors with private loans:

Direct-to-consumer (DTC) loans - often exceed "cost of attendance" and may be fully dischargeable.

Bar study loans - typically dischargeable under In re Campbell / McDaniel reasoning.

Mixed-use loans - fact-specific; the burden is on the creditor to prove qualified-loan status.

See private student loan dischargeability.

Montana Chapter 13 and Student Loans

In Chapter 13, student loans are generally paid pro-rata with other unsecured debt through the plan under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(1). The debtor may still file an adversary proceeding for discharge on undue hardship grounds, either during the case or after plan completion.

Practical advantages of the Chapter 13 path in Montana:

The automatic stay halts collection during the 3-5 year plan.

Accrued interest may be reduced through plan treatment.

A post-plan discharge adversary may succeed where a pre-plan one would not, because a completed plan is strong good-faith evidence.

See Chapter 13 and student loans.

Attorney Fees for Montana Adversary Proceedings

Student loan adversary proceedings carry fees in addition to the base Chapter 7 or 13 attorney fee. Typical Montana range: $2,000-$6,000 depending on case complexity and whether the loan holder contests discharge.

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 329(b), the bankruptcy court may review any attorney fee paid "in connection with" the case, including adversary-proceeding fees. Any fee paid for student loan litigation must be disclosed under Rule 2016(b) and is subject to the reasonableness standard. See Section 329 fee disgorgement overview.

Adversary proceeding mechanics

Private student loans

The cases below define the doctrine on this site:

McDaniel v. Navient Solutions, LLC, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020) - private student loans outside Section 523(a)(8) scope.

Rosenberg v. New York State Higher Educ. Servs. Corp., 610 B.R. 454 (S.D.N.Y. 2020) - seminal post-Brunner critique; catalyst for the 2022 DOJ attestation guidance.

Long v. Educational Credit Mgmt. Corp., 322 F.3d 549 (8th Cir. 2003) - totality-of-circumstances alternative.

## Student Loan Bankruptcy in Nebraska [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR
Source: https://bankruptcystudentloans.org/states/nebraska.html

← bankruptcystudentloans.org home

Student Loan Bankruptcy in Nebraska [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Nebraska residents.

Student Loan Discharge in Nebraska

Nebraska sits in the 8th Circuit, which does NOT use the rigid Brunner test. Instead, the 8th Circuit applies a totality-of-the-circumstances test that is generally considered more favorable to debtors seeking student loan discharge. Long v. ECMC, 322 F.3d 549 (8th Cir. 2003), is the controlling authority.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). To discharge them, the debtor must file an adversary proceeding within the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the test applied in the Eighth Circuit.

The Eighth Circuit Brunner Standard

Does NOT apply Brunner. Uses totality-of-the-circumstances test. Long v. ECMC, 322 F.3d 549 (8th Cir. 2003); Educational Credit Mgmt. Corp. v. Jesperson, 571 F.3d 775 (8th Cir. 2009). Significantly more debtor-friendly in theory.

Brunner (where it applies) requires the debtor to prove:

Minimal standard of living. That the debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and dependents if forced to repay the loans.

Persistence. That additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. That the debtor has made good faith efforts to repay the loans (including IDR/IBR enrollment, forbearances attempted, and payment history).

See the full Brunner test explanation.

In November 2022, the Department of Justice and Department of Education issued joint guidance that streamlines student loan discharge for federal loans. The guidance applies in every federal court, including those in Nebraska, and has materially increased discharge success rates.

Under the attestation process:

The debtor completes a standardized DOJ attestation form documenting income, expenses, and repayment history.

The DOJ reviews the attestation and, in most cases, supports discharge rather than contesting.

The underlying Brunner/totality analysis is applied, but with DOJ alignment.

The U.S. Trustee in Nebraska processes adversary proceedings consistent with this guidance. See adversary proceeding mechanics.

For Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) or Social Security Supplemental Security Income (SSI) recipients, federal loans qualify for Total and Permanent Disability (TPD) discharge without bankruptcy. Before filing an adversary proceeding, most courts in the Eighth Circuit require the debtor to show they have attempted income-driven repayment (IDR). Federal TPD primary path; state programs supplement.

Federal IDR plans available:

SAVE (formerly REPAYE) - 5-10% of discretionary income; lowest monthly payments for most debtors.

PAYE - 10% of discretionary income; 20-year forgiveness.

IBR - 10-15% of discretionary income; 20-25 year forgiveness.

ICR - 20% of discretionary income or 12-year standard, whichever less.

A Nebraska debtor at poverty-line income typically has a $0 monthly IDR payment under SAVE. This is important for the Brunner good-faith prong: you must show you tried IDR, not that IDR was impossible.

Private student loans are treated differently. Under the 10th Circuit's McDaniel v. Navient, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020), and similar reasoning in other circuits, a "qualified education loan" under 523(a)(8)(B) requires the funds to have been used solely for qualified educational expenses. Loans for living expenses, test preparation, or bar study may be dischargeable without proving undue hardship.

For Nebraska debtors with private loans:

Direct-to-consumer (DTC) loans - often exceed "cost of attendance" and may be fully dischargeable.

Bar study loans - typically dischargeable under In re Campbell / McDaniel reasoning.

Mixed-use loans - fact-specific; the burden is on the creditor to prove qualified-loan status.

See private student loan dischargeability.

The automatic stay halts collection during the 3-5 year plan.

A post-plan discharge adversary may succeed where a pre-plan one would not, because a completed plan is strong good-faith evidence.
