## Student Loan Bankruptcy in New Hampshire [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR
Source: https://bankruptcystudentloans.org/states/new-hampshire.html

← bankruptcystudentloans.org home

Student Loan Bankruptcy in New Hampshire [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for New Hampshire residents.

Student Loan Discharge in New Hampshire

New Hampshire sits in the 1st Circuit, which blends Brunner with totality-of-the-circumstances flexibility. Partial discharges and equitable considerations are more accessible than in strict-Brunner circuits.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). To discharge them, the debtor must file an adversary proceeding within the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the test applied in the First Circuit.

The First Circuit Brunner Standard

Uses a blend of Brunner and totality-of-circumstances. Bronsdon v. Educ. Credit Mgmt. Corp., 435 B.R. 791 (1st Cir. BAP 2010); In re Nash, 446 F.3d 188 (1st Cir. 2006) allows flexibility on the "additional circumstances" prong.

Brunner (where it applies) requires the debtor to prove:

Minimal standard of living. That the debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and dependents if forced to repay the loans.

Persistence. That additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. That the debtor has made good faith efforts to repay the loans (including IDR/IBR enrollment, forbearances attempted, and payment history).

## Student Loan Bankruptcy in New Jersey [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR
Source: https://bankruptcystudentloans.org/states/new-jersey.html

← bankruptcystudentloans.org home

Student Loan Bankruptcy in New Jersey [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for New Jersey residents.

Student Loan Discharge in New Jersey

New Jersey sits in the Third Circuit, which applies the Brunner three-prong test. Each prong must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence in an adversary proceeding.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). To discharge them, the debtor must file an adversary proceeding within the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the test applied in the Third Circuit.

The Third Circuit Brunner Standard

Applies Brunner. In re Faish, 72 F.3d 298 (3d Cir. 1995). Partial discharge permitted in some bankruptcy courts under In re Saxman logic.

Brunner (where it applies) requires the debtor to prove:

Minimal standard of living. That the debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and dependents if forced to repay the loans.

Persistence. That additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. That the debtor has made good faith efforts to repay the loans (including IDR/IBR enrollment, forbearances attempted, and payment history).

See the full Brunner test explanation.

DOJ/DOE Attestation Process (Nov 2022)

In November 2022, the Department of Justice and Department of Education issued joint guidance that streamlines student loan discharge for federal loans. The guidance applies in every federal court, including those in New Jersey, and has materially increased discharge success rates.

Under the attestation process:

The debtor completes a standardized DOJ attestation form documenting income, expenses, and repayment history.

The DOJ reviews the attestation and, in most cases, supports discharge rather than contesting.

The underlying Brunner/totality analysis is applied, but with DOJ alignment.

The U.S. Trustee in New Jersey processes adversary proceedings consistent with this guidance. See adversary proceeding mechanics.

New Jersey Disability and TPD Discharge

NJ Primary Care Physician/Dentist Loan Redemption; federal TPD. For Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) or Social Security Supplemental Security Income (SSI) recipients, federal loans qualify for Total and Permanent Disability (TPD) discharge without bankruptcy. TPD is administrative - no adversary proceeding needed - and applies to federal Direct, FFEL, and Perkins loans.

Three TPD qualification paths:

VA determination - Service-connected disability rated 100% or Individual Unemployability.

SSA determination - SSDI or SSI approval with a 5-7 year scheduled review flag.

Physician certification - M.D. or D.O. certifies that a medical impairment prevents substantial gainful activity.

TPD is the first path to check for any New Jersey debtor with a disability. Bankruptcy discharge is the fallback when TPD is unavailable or for private loans.

New Jersey Income-Driven Repayment Baseline

Before filing an adversary proceeding, most courts in the Third Circuit require the debtor to show they have attempted income-driven repayment (IDR). High COL adjusted in IDR; NJ loan redemption programs competitive.

Federal IDR plans available:

SAVE (formerly REPAYE) - 5-10% of discretionary income; lowest monthly payments for most debtors.

PAYE - 10% of discretionary income; 20-year forgiveness.

IBR - 10-15% of discretionary income; 20-25 year forgiveness.

ICR - 20% of discretionary income or 12-year standard, whichever less.

A New Jersey debtor at poverty-line income typically has a $0 monthly IDR payment under SAVE. This is important for the Brunner good-faith prong: you must show you tried IDR, not that IDR was impossible.

Private Student Loans in New Jersey

Private student loans are treated differently. Under the 10th Circuit's McDaniel v. Navient, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020), and similar reasoning in other circuits, a "qualified education loan" under 523(a)(8)(B) requires the funds to have been used solely for qualified educational expenses. Loans for living expenses, test preparation, or bar study may be dischargeable without proving undue hardship.

For New Jersey debtors with private loans:

Direct-to-consumer (DTC) loans - often exceed "cost of attendance" and may be fully dischargeable.

Bar study loans - typically dischargeable under In re Campbell / McDaniel reasoning.

Mixed-use loans - fact-specific; the burden is on the creditor to prove qualified-loan status.

See private student loan dischargeability.

New Jersey Federal Bankruptcy Data

Student loan adversary proceedings are filed within an underlying Chapter 7 or 13 case. The New Jersey consumer bankruptcy volume below shows the size of the pool where a 523(a)(8) complaint could be brought.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 1,580 consumer bankruptcy cases from New Jersey's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 752697.3%2.7%

Chapter 131,05431.0%68.8%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

New Jersey Chapter 13 and Student Loans

In Chapter 13, student loans are generally paid pro-rata with other unsecured debt through the plan under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(1). The debtor may still file an adversary proceeding for discharge on undue hardship grounds, either during the case or after plan completion.

Practical advantages of the Chapter 13 path in New Jersey:

The automatic stay halts collection during the 3-5 year plan.

Accrued interest may be reduced through plan treatment.

A post-plan discharge adversary may succeed where a pre-plan one would not, because a completed plan is strong good-faith evidence.

See Chapter 13 and student loans.

Attorney Fees for New Jersey Adversary Proceedings

Student loan adversary proceedings carry fees in addition to the base Chapter 7 or 13 attorney fee. Typical New Jersey range: $2,000-$6,000 depending on case complexity and whether the loan holder contests discharge.

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 329(b), the bankruptcy court may review any attorney fee paid "in connection with" the case, including adversary-proceeding fees. Any fee paid for student loan litigation must be disclosed under Rule 2016(b) and is subject to the reasonableness standard. See Section 329 fee disgorgement overview.

Related New Jersey Resources

Adversary proceeding mechanics

Chapter 13 and student loans

Private student loans

Student loan bankruptcy FAQ

Section 329 fee disgorgement

Foundational Caselaw

The cases below define the doctrine on this site:

Brunner v. New York State Higher Educ. Servs. Corp., 831 F.2d 395 (2d Cir. 1987) - origin of the three-prong undue-hardship test (per curiam).

McDaniel v. Navient Solutions, LLC, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020) - private student loans outside Section 523(a)(8) scope.

Rosenberg v. New York State Higher Educ. Servs. Corp., 610 B.R. 454 (S.D.N.Y. 2020) - seminal post-Brunner critique; catalyst for the 2022 DOJ attestation guidance.

Long v. Educational Credit Mgmt. Corp., 322 F.3d 549 (8th Cir. 2003) - totality-of-circumstances alternative.

## Student Loan Bankruptcy in New Mexico [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR
Source: https://bankruptcystudentloans.org/states/new-mexico.html

← bankruptcystudentloans.org home

Student Loan Bankruptcy in New Mexico [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for New Mexico residents.

Student Loan Discharge in New Mexico

New Mexico sits in the Tenth Circuit, which applies the Brunner three-prong test. Each prong must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence in an adversary proceeding.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). To discharge them, the debtor must file an adversary proceeding within the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the test applied in the Tenth Circuit.

The Tenth Circuit Brunner Standard

Applies Brunner. In re Woodcock, 45 F.3d 363 (10th Cir. 1995). Recent panels have loosened the good-faith prong; see McDaniel v. Navient (2020) on tuition-vs-educational distinction.

Brunner (where it applies) requires the debtor to prove:

Minimal standard of living. That the debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and dependents if forced to repay the loans.

Persistence. That additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. That the debtor has made good faith efforts to repay the loans (including IDR/IBR enrollment, forbearances attempted, and payment history).

See the full Brunner test explanation.

Under the attestation process:

The debtor completes a standardized DOJ attestation form documenting income, expenses, and repayment history.

The DOJ reviews the attestation and, in most cases, supports discharge rather than contesting.

The underlying Brunner/totality analysis is applied, but with DOJ alignment.

The U.S. Trustee in New Mexico processes adversary proceedings consistent with this guidance. See adversary proceeding mechanics.

Physician certification - M.D. or D.O. certifies that a medical impairment prevents substantial gainful activity.

TPD is the first path to check for any New Mexico debtor with a disability. Bankruptcy discharge is the fallback when TPD is unavailable or for private loans.

New Mexico Income-Driven Repayment Baseline

Before filing an adversary proceeding, most courts in the Tenth Circuit require the debtor to show they have attempted income-driven repayment (IDR). Below-median statewide; low IDR payments common.

Federal IDR plans available:

SAVE (formerly REPAYE) - 5-10% of discretionary income; lowest monthly payments for most debtors.

PAYE - 10% of discretionary income; 20-year forgiveness.

IBR - 10-15% of discretionary income; 20-25 year forgiveness.

ICR - 20% of discretionary income or 12-year standard, whichever less.

A New Mexico debtor at poverty-line income typically has a $0 monthly IDR payment under SAVE. This is important for the Brunner good-faith prong: you must show you tried IDR, not that IDR was impossible.

Loans for living expenses, test preparation, or bar study may be dischargeable without proving undue hardship.

For New Mexico debtors with private loans:

Direct-to-consumer (DTC) loans - often exceed "cost of attendance" and may be fully dischargeable.

Bar study loans - typically dischargeable under In re Campbell / McDaniel reasoning.

Mixed-use loans - fact-specific; the burden is on the creditor to prove qualified-loan status.

See private student loan dischargeability.

Practical advantages of the Chapter 13 path in New Mexico:

The automatic stay halts collection during the 3-5 year plan.

Accrued interest may be reduced through plan treatment.

A post-plan discharge adversary may succeed where a pre-plan one would not, because a completed plan is strong good-faith evidence.

See Chapter 13 and student loans.

Attorney Fees for New Mexico Adversary Proceedings

## Student Loan Bankruptcy in New York [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR
Source: https://bankruptcystudentloans.org/states/new-york.html

← bankruptcystudentloans.org home

Student Loan Bankruptcy in New York [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for New York residents.

Student Loan Discharge in New York

New York sits in the Second Circuit, which applies the Brunner three-prong test. Each prong must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence in an adversary proceeding.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). To discharge them, the debtor must file an adversary proceeding within the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the test applied in the Second Circuit.

The Second Circuit Brunner Standard

Adopted Brunner originally (the test is named after a 2d Circuit case). Strict three-prong application. Brunner v. New York State Higher Educ. Servs. Corp., 831 F.2d 395 (2d Cir. 1987). Good-faith prong heavily scrutinized.

Brunner (where it applies) requires the debtor to prove:

Minimal standard of living. That the debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and dependents if forced to repay the loans.

Persistence. That additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. That the debtor has made good faith efforts to repay the loans (including IDR/IBR enrollment, forbearances attempted, and payment history).

See the full Brunner test explanation.

In November 2022, the Department of Justice and Department of Education issued joint guidance that streamlines student loan discharge for federal loans. The guidance applies in every federal court, including those in New York, and has materially increased discharge success rates.

Under the attestation process:

The debtor completes a standardized DOJ attestation form documenting income, expenses, and repayment history.

The DOJ reviews the attestation and, in most cases, supports discharge rather than contesting.

The underlying Brunner/totality analysis is applied, but with DOJ alignment.

The U.S. Trustee in New York processes adversary proceedings consistent with this guidance. See adversary proceeding mechanics.

New York Disability and TPD Discharge

NY Regents Physician Loan Forgiveness, Nurse Faculty, and others; federal TPD. For Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) or Social Security Supplemental Security Income (SSI) recipients, federal loans qualify for Total and Permanent Disability (TPD) discharge without bankruptcy. TPD is administrative - no adversary proceeding needed - and applies to federal Direct, FFEL, and Perkins loans.

Three TPD qualification paths:

Physician certification - M.D. or D.O. certifies that a medical impairment prevents substantial gainful activity.

TPD is the first path to check for any New York debtor with a disability. Bankruptcy discharge is the fallback when TPD is unavailable or for private loans.

New York Income-Driven Repayment Baseline

Before filing an adversary proceeding, most courts in the Second Circuit require the debtor to show they have attempted income-driven repayment (IDR). NY has robust state-level forgiveness; NYC COL adjustment high in IDR.

Federal IDR plans available:

SAVE (formerly REPAYE) - 5-10% of discretionary income; lowest monthly payments for most debtors.

PAYE - 10% of discretionary income; 20-year forgiveness.

IBR - 10-15% of discretionary income; 20-25 year forgiveness.

ICR - 20% of discretionary income or 12-year standard, whichever less.

A New York debtor at poverty-line income typically has a $0 monthly IDR payment under SAVE. This is important for the Brunner good-faith prong: you must show you tried IDR, not that IDR was impossible.

Private Student Loans in New York

Private student loans are treated differently. Under the 10th Circuit's McDaniel v. Navient, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020), and similar reasoning in other circuits, a "qualified education loan" under 523(a)(8)(B) requires the funds to have been used solely for qualified educational expenses. Loans for living expenses, test preparation, or bar study may be dischargeable without proving undue hardship.

For New York debtors with private loans:

Direct-to-consumer (DTC) loans - often exceed "cost of attendance" and may be fully dischargeable.

Bar study loans - typically dischargeable under In re Campbell / McDaniel reasoning.

Mixed-use loans - fact-specific; the burden is on the creditor to prove qualified-loan status.

See private student loan dischargeability.

Student loan adversary proceedings are filed within an underlying Chapter 7 or 13 case. The New York consumer bankruptcy volume below shows the size of the pool where a 523(a)(8) complaint could be brought.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 1,231 consumer bankruptcy cases from New York's federal bankruptcy courts.

In Chapter 13, student loans are generally paid pro-rata with other unsecured debt through the plan under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(1). The debtor may still file an adversary proceeding for discharge on undue hardship grounds, either during the case or after plan completion.

Practical advantages of the Chapter 13 path in New York:

The automatic stay halts collection during the 3-5 year plan.

Accrued interest may be reduced through plan treatment.

A post-plan discharge adversary may succeed where a pre-plan one would not, because a completed plan is strong good-faith evidence.

See Chapter 13 and student loans.

Attorney Fees for New York Adversary Proceedings

Student loan adversary proceedings carry fees in addition to the base Chapter 7 or 13 attorney fee. Typical New York range: $2,000-$6,000 depending on case complexity and whether the loan holder contests discharge.

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 329(b), the bankruptcy court may review any attorney fee paid "in connection with" the case, including adversary-proceeding fees. Any fee paid for student loan litigation must be disclosed under Rule 2016(b) and is subject to the reasonableness standard. See Section 329 fee disgorgement overview.

## Student Loan Bankruptcy in North Carolina [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR
Source: https://bankruptcystudentloans.org/states/north-carolina.html

← bankruptcystudentloans.org home

Student Loan Bankruptcy in North Carolina [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for North Carolina residents.

Student Loan Discharge in North Carolina

North Carolina sits in the Fourth Circuit, which applies the Brunner three-prong test. Each prong must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence in an adversary proceeding.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). To discharge them, the debtor must file an adversary proceeding within the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the test applied in the Fourth Circuit.

The Fourth Circuit Brunner Standard

Applies Brunner. In re Frushour, 433 F.3d 393 (4th Cir. 2005). Strict good-faith inquiry; debtors expected to document IBR/IDR attempts.

Brunner (where it applies) requires the debtor to prove:

Minimal standard of living. That the debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and dependents if forced to repay the loans.

Persistence. That additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. That the debtor has made good faith efforts to repay the loans (including IDR/IBR enrollment, forbearances attempted, and payment history).

## Student Loan Bankruptcy in North Dakota [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR
Source: https://bankruptcystudentloans.org/states/north-dakota.html

← bankruptcystudentloans.org home

Student Loan Bankruptcy in North Dakota [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for North Dakota residents.

Student Loan Discharge in North Dakota

North Dakota sits in the 8th Circuit, which does NOT use the rigid Brunner test. Instead, the 8th Circuit applies a totality-of-the-circumstances test that is generally considered more favorable to debtors seeking student loan discharge. Long v. ECMC, 322 F.3d 549 (8th Cir. 2003), is the controlling authority.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). To discharge them, the debtor must file an adversary proceeding within the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the test applied in the Eighth Circuit.

The Eighth Circuit Brunner Standard

Does NOT apply Brunner. Uses totality-of-the-circumstances test. Long v. ECMC, 322 F.3d 549 (8th Cir. 2003); Educational Credit Mgmt. Corp. v. Jesperson, 571 F.3d 775 (8th Cir. 2009). Significantly more debtor-friendly in theory.

Brunner (where it applies) requires the debtor to prove:

Minimal standard of living. That the debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and dependents if forced to repay the loans.

Persistence. That additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. That the debtor has made good faith efforts to repay the loans (including IDR/IBR enrollment, forbearances attempted, and payment history).

See the full Brunner test explanation.

DOJ/DOE Attestation Process (Nov 2022)

In November 2022, the Department of Justice and Department of Education issued joint guidance that streamlines student loan discharge for federal loans. The guidance applies in every federal court, including those in North Dakota, and has materially increased discharge success rates.

Under the attestation process:

The debtor completes a standardized DOJ attestation form documenting income, expenses, and repayment history.

The DOJ reviews the attestation and, in most cases, supports discharge rather than contesting.

The underlying Brunner/totality analysis is applied, but with DOJ alignment.

The U.S. Trustee in North Dakota processes adversary proceedings consistent with this guidance. See adversary proceeding mechanics.

North Dakota Disability and TPD Discharge

ND Professional Loan Repayment; federal TPD. For Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) or Social Security Supplemental Security Income (SSI) recipients, federal loans qualify for Total and Permanent Disability (TPD) discharge without bankruptcy. TPD is administrative - no adversary proceeding needed - and applies to federal Direct, FFEL, and Perkins loans.

Three TPD qualification paths:

VA determination - Service-connected disability rated 100% or Individual Unemployability.

SSA determination - SSDI or SSI approval with a 5-7 year scheduled review flag.

Physician certification - M.D. or D.O. certifies that a medical impairment prevents substantial gainful activity.

TPD is the first path to check for any North Dakota debtor with a disability. Bankruptcy discharge is the fallback when TPD is unavailable or for private loans.

North Dakota Income-Driven Repayment Baseline

Before filing an adversary proceeding, most courts in the Eighth Circuit require the debtor to show they have attempted income-driven repayment (IDR). Low population; federal programs cover most debtors.

Federal IDR plans available:

SAVE (formerly REPAYE) - 5-10% of discretionary income; lowest monthly payments for most debtors.

PAYE - 10% of discretionary income; 20-year forgiveness.

IBR - 10-15% of discretionary income; 20-25 year forgiveness.

ICR - 20% of discretionary income or 12-year standard, whichever less.

A North Dakota debtor at poverty-line income typically has a $0 monthly IDR payment under SAVE. This is important for the Brunner good-faith prong: you must show you tried IDR, not that IDR was impossible.

Private Student Loans in North Dakota

Private student loans are treated differently. Under the 10th Circuit's McDaniel v. Navient, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020), and similar reasoning in other circuits, a "qualified education loan" under 523(a)(8)(B) requires the funds to have been used solely for qualified educational expenses. Loans for living expenses, test preparation, or bar study may be dischargeable without proving undue hardship.

For North Dakota debtors with private loans:

Direct-to-consumer (DTC) loans - often exceed "cost of attendance" and may be fully dischargeable.

Bar study loans - typically dischargeable under In re Campbell / McDaniel reasoning.

Mixed-use loans - fact-specific; the burden is on the creditor to prove qualified-loan status.

See private student loan dischargeability.

North Dakota Chapter 13 and Student Loans

In Chapter 13, student loans are generally paid pro-rata with other unsecured debt through the plan under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(1). The debtor may still file an adversary proceeding for discharge on undue hardship grounds, either during the case or after plan completion.

Practical advantages of the Chapter 13 path in North Dakota:

The automatic stay halts collection during the 3-5 year plan.

Accrued interest may be reduced through plan treatment.

A post-plan discharge adversary may succeed where a pre-plan one would not, because a completed plan is strong good-faith evidence.

See Chapter 13 and student loans.

Attorney Fees for North Dakota Adversary Proceedings

Student loan adversary proceedings carry fees in addition to the base Chapter 7 or 13 attorney fee. Typical North Dakota range: $2,000-$6,000 depending on case complexity and whether the loan holder contests discharge.

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 329(b), the bankruptcy court may review any attorney fee paid "in connection with" the case, including adversary-proceeding fees. Any fee paid for student loan litigation must be disclosed under Rule 2016(b) and is subject to the reasonableness standard. See Section 329 fee disgorgement overview.

Foundational Caselaw

The cases below define the doctrine on this site:

Brunner v. New York State Higher Educ. Servs. Corp., 831 F.2d 395 (2d Cir. 1987) - origin of the three-prong undue-hardship test (per curiam).

McDaniel v. Navient Solutions, LLC, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020) - private student loans outside Section 523(a)(8) scope.

Rosenberg v. New York State Higher Educ. Servs. Corp., 610 B.R. 454 (S.D.N.Y. 2020) - seminal post-Brunner critique; catalyst for the 2022 DOJ attestation guidance.

Long v. Educational Credit Mgmt. Corp., 322 F.3d 549 (8th Cir. 2003) - totality-of-circumstances alternative.

## Student Loan Bankruptcy in Ohio [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR
Source: https://bankruptcystudentloans.org/states/ohio.html

← bankruptcystudentloans.org home

Student Loan Bankruptcy in Ohio [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Ohio residents.

Student Loan Discharge in Ohio

Ohio sits in the Sixth Circuit, which applies the Brunner three-prong test. Each prong must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence in an adversary proceeding.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). To discharge them, the debtor must file an adversary proceeding within the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the test applied in the Sixth Circuit.

The Sixth Circuit Brunner Standard

Applies Brunner. In re Oyler, 397 F.3d 382 (6th Cir. 2005). Good-faith considered based on repayment history and lifestyle choices.

Brunner (where it applies) requires the debtor to prove:

Minimal standard of living. That the debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and dependents if forced to repay the loans.

Persistence. That additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. That the debtor has made good faith efforts to repay the loans (including IDR/IBR enrollment, forbearances attempted, and payment history).

See the full Brunner test explanation.

The DOJ reviews the attestation and, in most cases, supports discharge rather than contesting.

The underlying Brunner/totality analysis is applied, but with DOJ alignment.

Before filing an adversary proceeding, most courts in the Sixth Circuit require the debtor to show they have attempted income-driven repayment (IDR). Standard 6th Cir. Brunner; expense substantiation important.

Federal IDR plans available:

SAVE (formerly REPAYE) - 5-10% of discretionary income; lowest monthly payments for most debtors.

PAYE - 10% of discretionary income; 20-year forgiveness.

IBR - 10-15% of discretionary income; 20-25 year forgiveness.

ICR - 20% of discretionary income or 12-year standard, whichever less.

Bar study loans - typically dischargeable under In re Campbell / McDaniel reasoning.

Mixed-use loans - fact-specific; the burden is on the creditor to prove qualified-loan status.

See private student loan dischargeability.

Minimal standard of living. That the debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and dependents if forced to repay the loans.

## Student Loan Bankruptcy in Oregon [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR
Source: https://bankruptcystudentloans.org/states/oregon.html

← bankruptcystudentloans.org home

Student Loan Bankruptcy in Oregon [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Oregon residents.

Student Loan Discharge in Oregon

Oregon sits in the 9th Circuit, which applies Brunner with the Pena gloss. Partial discharges are available, and the DOJ/DOE November 2022 guidance is well-integrated in 9th Circuit practice.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). To discharge them, the debtor must file an adversary proceeding within the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the test applied in the Ninth Circuit.

The Ninth Circuit Brunner Standard

Applies Brunner. In re Pena, 155 F.3d 1108 (9th Cir. 1998). Allows partial discharge and considers payment-history attempts favorably under DOJ/DOE guidance.

Brunner (where it applies) requires the debtor to prove:

Minimal standard of living. That the debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and dependents if forced to repay the loans.

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Pennsylvania residents.

Pennsylvania sits in the Third Circuit, which applies the Brunner three-prong test. Each prong must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence in an adversary proceeding.

Persistence. That additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

TPD is administrative - no adversary proceeding needed - and applies to federal Direct, FFEL, and Perkins loans.

Three TPD qualification paths:

VA determination - Service-connected disability rated 100% or Individual Unemployability.

SSA determination - SSDI or SSI approval with a 5-7 year scheduled review flag.

Physician certification - M.D. or D.O. certifies that a medical impairment prevents substantial gainful activity.

TPD is the first path to check for any Pennsylvania debtor with a disability. Bankruptcy discharge is the fallback when TPD is unavailable or for private loans.

Pennsylvania Income-Driven Repayment Baseline

Before filing an adversary proceeding, most courts in the Third Circuit require the debtor to show they have attempted income-driven repayment (IDR). 3rd Cir. Brunner; Faish the leading case.

Federal IDR plans available:

SAVE (formerly REPAYE) - 5-10% of discretionary income; lowest monthly payments for most debtors.

PAYE - 10% of discretionary income; 20-year forgiveness.

IBR - 10-15% of discretionary income; 20-25 year forgiveness.

ICR - 20% of discretionary income or 12-year standard, whichever less.

A Pennsylvania debtor at poverty-line income typically has a $0 monthly IDR payment under SAVE. This is important for the Brunner good-faith prong: you must show you tried IDR, not that IDR was impossible.

Private Student Loans in Pennsylvania

Private student loans are treated differently. Under the 10th Circuit's McDaniel v. Navient, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020), and similar reasoning in other circuits, a "qualified education loan" under 523(a)(8)(B) requires the funds to have been used solely for qualified educational expenses. Loans for living expenses, test preparation, or bar study may be dischargeable without proving undue hardship.

For Pennsylvania debtors with private loans:

Direct-to-consumer (DTC) loans - often exceed "cost of attendance" and may be fully dischargeable.

Bar study loans - typically dischargeable under In re Campbell / McDaniel reasoning.

Mixed-use loans - fact-specific; the burden is on the creditor to prove qualified-loan status.

See private student loan dischargeability.

Pennsylvania Federal Bankruptcy Data

Student loan adversary proceedings are filed within an underlying Chapter 7 or 13 case. The Pennsylvania consumer bankruptcy volume below shows the size of the pool where a 523(a)(8) complaint could be brought.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 1,513 consumer bankruptcy cases from Pennsylvania's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 7415n/an/a

Chapter 131,098n/an/a

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Pennsylvania Chapter 13 and Student Loans

In Chapter 13, student loans are generally paid pro-rata with other unsecured debt through the plan under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(1). The debtor may still file an adversary proceeding for discharge on undue hardship grounds, either during the case or after plan completion.

Practical advantages of the Chapter 13 path in Pennsylvania:

The automatic stay halts collection during the 3-5 year plan.

Accrued interest may be reduced through plan treatment.

A post-plan discharge adversary may succeed where a pre-plan one would not, because a completed plan is strong good-faith evidence.

See Chapter 13 and student loans.

Attorney Fees for Pennsylvania Adversary Proceedings

Student loan adversary proceedings carry fees in addition to the base Chapter 7 or 13 attorney fee. Typical Pennsylvania range: $2,000-$6,000 depending on case complexity and whether the loan holder contests discharge.

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 329(b), the bankruptcy court may review any attorney fee paid "in connection with" the case, including adversary-proceeding fees. Any fee paid for student loan litigation must be disclosed under Rule 2016(b) and is subject to the reasonableness standard. See Section 329 fee disgorgement overview.

The cases below define the doctrine on this site:

Rosenberg v. New York State Higher Educ. Servs. Corp., 610 B.R. 454 (S.D.N.Y. 2020) - seminal post-Brunner critique; catalyst for the 2022 DOJ attestation guidance.

## Student Loan Bankruptcy in Rhode Island [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR
Source: https://bankruptcystudentloans.org/states/rhode-island.html

← bankruptcystudentloans.org home

Student Loan Bankruptcy in Rhode Island [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Rhode Island residents.

Student Loan Discharge in Rhode Island

Rhode Island sits in the 1st Circuit, which blends Brunner with totality-of-the-circumstances flexibility. Partial discharges and equitable considerations are more accessible than in strict-Brunner circuits.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). To discharge them, the debtor must file an adversary proceeding within the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the test applied in the First Circuit.

The First Circuit Brunner Standard

Uses a blend of Brunner and totality-of-circumstances. Bronsdon v. Educ. Credit Mgmt. Corp., 435 B.R. 791 (1st Cir. BAP 2010); In re Nash, 446 F.3d 188 (1st Cir. 2006) allows flexibility on the "additional circumstances" prong.

Brunner (where it applies) requires the debtor to prove:

Minimal standard of living. That the debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and dependents if forced to repay the loans.

Persistence. That additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. That the debtor has made good faith efforts to repay the loans (including IDR/IBR enrollment, forbearances attempted, and payment history).

See the full Brunner test explanation.

DOJ/DOE Attestation Process (Nov 2022)

In November 2022, the Department of Justice and Department of Education issued joint guidance that streamlines student loan discharge for federal loans. The guidance applies in every federal court, including those in Rhode Island, and has materially increased discharge success rates.

Under the attestation process:

The debtor completes a standardized DOJ attestation form documenting income, expenses, and repayment history.

The DOJ reviews the attestation and, in most cases, supports discharge rather than contesting.

The underlying Brunner/totality analysis is applied, but with DOJ alignment.

The U.S. Trustee in Rhode Island processes adversary proceedings consistent with this guidance. See adversary proceeding mechanics.

Rhode Island Disability and TPD Discharge

RI Health Professional Loan Repayment; federal TPD. For Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) or Social Security Supplemental Security Income (SSI) recipients, federal loans qualify for Total and Permanent Disability (TPD) discharge without bankruptcy. TPD is administrative - no adversary proceeding needed - and applies to federal Direct, FFEL, and Perkins loans.

Three TPD qualification paths:

VA determination - Service-connected disability rated 100% or Individual Unemployability.

SSA determination - SSDI or SSI approval with a 5-7 year scheduled review flag.

Physician certification - M.D. or D.O. certifies that a medical impairment prevents substantial gainful activity.

TPD is the first path to check for any Rhode Island debtor with a disability. Bankruptcy discharge is the fallback when TPD is unavailable or for private loans.

Rhode Island Income-Driven Repayment Baseline

Before filing an adversary proceeding, most courts in the First Circuit require the debtor to show they have attempted income-driven repayment (IDR). Small state; federal TPD and PSLF central.

Federal IDR plans available:

SAVE (formerly REPAYE) - 5-10% of discretionary income; lowest monthly payments for most debtors.

PAYE - 10% of discretionary income; 20-year forgiveness.

IBR - 10-15% of discretionary income; 20-25 year forgiveness.

ICR - 20% of discretionary income or 12-year standard, whichever less.

A Rhode Island debtor at poverty-line income typically has a $0 monthly IDR payment under SAVE. This is important for the Brunner good-faith prong: you must show you tried IDR, not that IDR was impossible.

Private Student Loans in Rhode Island

Private student loans are treated differently. Under the 10th Circuit's McDaniel v. Navient, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020), and similar reasoning in other circuits, a "qualified education loan" under 523(a)(8)(B) requires the funds to have been used solely for qualified educational expenses. Loans for living expenses, test preparation, or bar study may be dischargeable without proving undue hardship.

For Rhode Island debtors with private loans:

Direct-to-consumer (DTC) loans - often exceed "cost of attendance" and may be fully dischargeable.

Bar study loans - typically dischargeable under In re Campbell / McDaniel reasoning.

Mixed-use loans - fact-specific; the burden is on the creditor to prove qualified-loan status.

See private student loan dischargeability.

Rhode Island Chapter 13 and Student Loans

In Chapter 13, student loans are generally paid pro-rata with other unsecured debt through the plan under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(1). The debtor may still file an adversary proceeding for discharge on undue hardship grounds, either during the case or after plan completion.

Practical advantages of the Chapter 13 path in Rhode Island:

The automatic stay halts collection during the 3-5 year plan.

Accrued interest may be reduced through plan treatment.

A post-plan discharge adversary may succeed where a pre-plan one would not, because a completed plan is strong good-faith evidence.

See Chapter 13 and student loans.

Attorney Fees for Rhode Island Adversary Proceedings

Student loan adversary proceedings carry fees in addition to the base Chapter 7 or 13 attorney fee. Typical Rhode Island range: $2,000-$6,000 depending on case complexity and whether the loan holder contests discharge.

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 329(b), the bankruptcy court may review any attorney fee paid "in connection with" the case, including adversary-proceeding fees. Any fee paid for student loan litigation must be disclosed under Rule 2016(b) and is subject to the reasonableness standard. See Section 329 fee disgorgement overview.

## Student Loan Bankruptcy in South Carolina [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR
Source: https://bankruptcystudentloans.org/states/south-carolina.html

← bankruptcystudentloans.org home

Student Loan Bankruptcy in South Carolina [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for South Carolina residents.

Student Loan Discharge in South Carolina

South Carolina sits in the Fourth Circuit, which applies the Brunner three-prong test. Each prong must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence in an adversary proceeding.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). To discharge them, the debtor must file an adversary proceeding within the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the test applied in the Fourth Circuit.

The Fourth Circuit Brunner Standard

Applies Brunner. In re Frushour, 433 F.3d 393 (4th Cir. 2005). Strict good-faith inquiry; debtors expected to document IBR/IDR attempts.

Brunner (where it applies) requires the debtor to prove:

Minimal standard of living. That the debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and dependents if forced to repay the loans.

Persistence. That additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. That the debtor has made good faith efforts to repay the loans (including IDR/IBR enrollment, forbearances attempted, and payment history).

See the full Brunner test explanation.

The debtor completes a standardized DOJ attestation form documenting income, expenses, and repayment history.

The DOJ reviews the attestation and, in most cases, supports discharge rather than contesting.

Federal IDR plans available:

SAVE (formerly REPAYE) - 5-10% of discretionary income; lowest monthly payments for most debtors.

PAYE - 10% of discretionary income; 20-year forgiveness.

IBR - 10-15% of discretionary income; 20-25 year forgiveness.

## Student Loan Bankruptcy in South Dakota [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR
Source: https://bankruptcystudentloans.org/states/south-dakota.html

← bankruptcystudentloans.org home

Student Loan Bankruptcy in South Dakota [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for South Dakota residents.

Student Loan Discharge in South Dakota

South Dakota sits in the 8th Circuit, which does NOT use the rigid Brunner test. Instead, the 8th Circuit applies a totality-of-the-circumstances test that is generally considered more favorable to debtors seeking student loan discharge. Long v. ECMC, 322 F.3d 549 (8th Cir. 2003), is the controlling authority.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). To discharge them, the debtor must file an adversary proceeding within the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the test applied in the Eighth Circuit.

The Eighth Circuit Brunner Standard

Does NOT apply Brunner. Uses totality-of-the-circumstances test. Long v. ECMC, 322 F.3d 549 (8th Cir. 2003); Educational Credit Mgmt. Corp. v. Jesperson, 571 F.3d 775 (8th Cir. 2009). Significantly more debtor-friendly in theory.

Brunner (where it applies) requires the debtor to prove:

Minimal standard of living. That the debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and dependents if forced to repay the loans.

Persistence. That additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. That the debtor has made good faith efforts to repay the loans (including IDR/IBR enrollment, forbearances attempted, and payment history).

← bankruptcystudentloans.org home

Student Loan Bankruptcy in Tennessee [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Tennessee residents.

Applies Brunner. In re Oyler, 397 F.3d 382 (6th Cir. 2005). Good-faith considered based on repayment history and lifestyle choices.

Brunner (where it applies) requires the debtor to prove:

Minimal standard of living. That the debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and dependents if forced to repay the loans.

Persistence. That additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Loans for living expenses, test preparation, or bar study may be dischargeable without proving undue hardship.

For Tennessee debtors with private loans:

Direct-to-consumer (DTC) loans - often exceed "cost of attendance" and may be fully dischargeable.

Bar study loans - typically dischargeable under In re Campbell / McDaniel reasoning.

Mixed-use loans - fact-specific; the burden is on the creditor to prove qualified-loan status.

See private student loan dischargeability.

Tennessee Federal Bankruptcy Data

Student loan adversary proceedings are filed within an underlying Chapter 7 or 13 case. The Tennessee consumer bankruptcy volume below shows the size of the pool where a 523(a)(8) complaint could be brought.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 1,840 consumer bankruptcy cases from Tennessee's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 758995.5%4.5%

Chapter 131,25117.3%82.7%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Tennessee Chapter 13 and Student Loans

In Chapter 13, student loans are generally paid pro-rata with other unsecured debt through the plan under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(1). The debtor may still file an adversary proceeding for discharge on undue hardship grounds, either during the case or after plan completion.

Practical advantages of the Chapter 13 path in Tennessee:

The automatic stay halts collection during the 3-5 year plan.

Accrued interest may be reduced through plan treatment.

A post-plan discharge adversary may succeed where a pre-plan one would not, because a completed plan is strong good-faith evidence.

See Chapter 13 and student loans.

Attorney Fees for Tennessee Adversary Proceedings

Student loan adversary proceedings carry fees in addition to the base Chapter 7 or 13 attorney fee. Typical Tennessee range: $2,000-$6,000 depending on case complexity and whether the loan holder contests discharge.

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 329(b), the bankruptcy court may review any attorney fee paid "in connection with" the case, including adversary-proceeding fees. Any fee paid for student loan litigation must be disclosed under Rule 2016(b) and is subject to the reasonableness standard. See Section 329 fee disgorgement overview.

## Student Loan Bankruptcy in Texas [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR
Source: https://bankruptcystudentloans.org/states/texas.html

← bankruptcystudentloans.org home

Student Loan Bankruptcy in Texas [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Texas residents.

Student Loan Discharge in Texas

Texas sits in the Fifth Circuit, which applies the Brunner three-prong test. Each prong must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence in an adversary proceeding.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). To discharge them, the debtor must file an adversary proceeding within the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the test applied in the Fifth Circuit.

The Fifth Circuit Brunner Standard

Applies Brunner. In re Gerhardt, 348 F.3d 89 (5th Cir. 2003). Historically strict; the 2019 Thomas decision narrowed "minimal standard of living" but also reaffirmed Brunner.

Brunner (where it applies) requires the debtor to prove:

Minimal standard of living. That the debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and dependents if forced to repay the loans.

Persistence. That additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. That the debtor has made good faith efforts to repay the loans (including IDR/IBR enrollment, forbearances attempted, and payment history).

See the full Brunner test explanation.

DOJ/DOE Attestation Process (Nov 2022)

In November 2022, the Department of Justice and Department of Education issued joint guidance that streamlines student loan discharge for federal loans. The guidance applies in every federal court, including those in Texas, and has materially increased discharge success rates.

Under the attestation process:

The debtor completes a standardized DOJ attestation form documenting income, expenses, and repayment history.

The DOJ reviews the attestation and, in most cases, supports discharge rather than contesting.

The underlying Brunner/totality analysis is applied, but with DOJ alignment.

The U.S. Trustee in Texas processes adversary proceedings consistent with this guidance. See adversary proceeding mechanics.

Texas Disability and TPD Discharge

TX Physician Education Loan Repayment, Teach for Texas; federal TPD. For Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) or Social Security Supplemental Security Income (SSI) recipients, federal loans qualify for Total and Permanent Disability (TPD) discharge without bankruptcy. TPD is administrative - no adversary proceeding needed - and applies to federal Direct, FFEL, and Perkins loans.

Three TPD qualification paths:

VA determination - Service-connected disability rated 100% or Individual Unemployability.

SSA determination - SSDI or SSI approval with a 5-7 year scheduled review flag.

Physician certification - M.D. or D.O. certifies that a medical impairment prevents substantial gainful activity.

TPD is the first path to check for any Texas debtor with a disability. Bankruptcy discharge is the fallback when TPD is unavailable or for private loans.

Texas Income-Driven Repayment Baseline

Before filing an adversary proceeding, most courts in the Fifth Circuit require the debtor to show they have attempted income-driven repayment (IDR). 5th Cir. Brunner; Gerhardt and Thomas control.

Federal IDR plans available:

SAVE (formerly REPAYE) - 5-10% of discretionary income; lowest monthly payments for most debtors.

PAYE - 10% of discretionary income; 20-year forgiveness.

IBR - 10-15% of discretionary income; 20-25 year forgiveness.

ICR - 20% of discretionary income or 12-year standard, whichever less.

A Texas debtor at poverty-line income typically has a $0 monthly IDR payment under SAVE. This is important for the Brunner good-faith prong: you must show you tried IDR, not that IDR was impossible.

Private Student Loans in Texas

Private student loans are treated differently. Under the 10th Circuit's McDaniel v. Navient, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020), and similar reasoning in other circuits, a "qualified education loan" under 523(a)(8)(B) requires the funds to have been used solely for qualified educational expenses. Loans for living expenses, test preparation, or bar study may be dischargeable without proving undue hardship.

For Texas debtors with private loans:

Direct-to-consumer (DTC) loans - often exceed "cost of attendance" and may be fully dischargeable.

Bar study loans - typically dischargeable under In re Campbell / McDaniel reasoning.

Mixed-use loans - fact-specific; the burden is on the creditor to prove qualified-loan status.

See private student loan dischargeability.

Texas Federal Bankruptcy Data

Student loan adversary proceedings are filed within an underlying Chapter 7 or 13 case. The Texas consumer bankruptcy volume below shows the size of the pool where a 523(a)(8) complaint could be brought.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 30,781 consumer bankruptcy cases from Texas's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 711,84497.8%2.0%

Chapter 1318,93736.8%63.2%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Texas Chapter 13 and Student Loans

In Chapter 13, student loans are generally paid pro-rata with other unsecured debt through the plan under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(1). The debtor may still file an adversary proceeding for discharge on undue hardship grounds, either during the case or after plan completion.

Practical advantages of the Chapter 13 path in Texas:

The automatic stay halts collection during the 3-5 year plan.

Accrued interest may be reduced through plan treatment.

A post-plan discharge adversary may succeed where a pre-plan one would not, because a completed plan is strong good-faith evidence.

See Chapter 13 and student loans.

Attorney Fees for Texas Adversary Proceedings

Student loan adversary proceedings carry fees in addition to the base Chapter 7 or 13 attorney fee. Typical Texas range: $2,000-$6,000 depending on case complexity and whether the loan holder contests discharge.

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 329(b), the bankruptcy court may review any attorney fee paid "in connection with" the case, including adversary-proceeding fees. Any fee paid for student loan litigation must be disclosed under Rule 2016(b) and is subject to the reasonableness standard. See Section 329 fee disgorgement overview.

Source: https://bankruptcystudentloans.org/states/vermont.html

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Vermont residents.

The Second Circuit Brunner Standard

Brunner (where it applies) requires the debtor to prove:

Minimal standard of living. That the debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and dependents if forced to repay the loans.

Source: https://bankruptcystudentloans.org/states/virginia.html

## Student Loan Bankruptcy in Washington [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR
Source: https://bankruptcystudentloans.org/states/washington.html

← bankruptcystudentloans.org home

Student Loan Bankruptcy in Washington [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Washington residents.

Student Loan Discharge in Washington

Washington sits in the 9th Circuit, which applies Brunner with the Pena gloss. Partial discharges are available, and the DOJ/DOE November 2022 guidance is well-integrated in 9th Circuit practice.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). To discharge them, the debtor must file an adversary proceeding within the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the test applied in the Ninth Circuit.

The Ninth Circuit Brunner Standard

Applies Brunner. In re Pena, 155 F.3d 1108 (9th Cir. 1998). Allows partial discharge and considers payment-history attempts favorably under DOJ/DOE guidance.

Brunner (where it applies) requires the debtor to prove:

Minimal standard of living. That the debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and dependents if forced to repay the loans.

Persistence. That additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. That the debtor has made good faith efforts to repay the loans (including IDR/IBR enrollment, forbearances attempted, and payment history).

See the full Brunner test explanation.

DOJ/DOE Attestation Process (Nov 2022)

In November 2022, the Department of Justice and Department of Education issued joint guidance that streamlines student loan discharge for federal loans. The guidance applies in every federal court, including those in Washington, and has materially increased discharge success rates.

Under the attestation process:

The debtor completes a standardized DOJ attestation form documenting income, expenses, and repayment history.

The DOJ reviews the attestation and, in most cases, supports discharge rather than contesting.

The underlying Brunner/totality analysis is applied, but with DOJ alignment.

The U.S. Trustee in Washington processes adversary proceedings consistent with this guidance. See adversary proceeding mechanics.

Washington Disability and TPD Discharge

WA Health Professional Loan Repayment; federal TPD. For Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) or Social Security Supplemental Security Income (SSI) recipients, federal loans qualify for Total and Permanent Disability (TPD) discharge without bankruptcy. TPD is administrative - no adversary proceeding needed - and applies to federal Direct, FFEL, and Perkins loans.

Three TPD qualification paths:

VA determination - Service-connected disability rated 100% or Individual Unemployability.

SSA determination - SSDI or SSI approval with a 5-7 year scheduled review flag.

Physician certification - M.D. or D.O. certifies that a medical impairment prevents substantial gainful activity.

TPD is the first path to check for any Washington debtor with a disability. Bankruptcy discharge is the fallback when TPD is unavailable or for private loans.

Washington Income-Driven Repayment Baseline

Before filing an adversary proceeding, most courts in the Ninth Circuit require the debtor to show they have attempted income-driven repayment (IDR). 9th Cir. Pena-style partial discharges available.

Federal IDR plans available:

SAVE (formerly REPAYE) - 5-10% of discretionary income; lowest monthly payments for most debtors.

PAYE - 10% of discretionary income; 20-year forgiveness.

IBR - 10-15% of discretionary income; 20-25 year forgiveness.

ICR - 20% of discretionary income or 12-year standard, whichever less.

A Washington debtor at poverty-line income typically has a $0 monthly IDR payment under SAVE. This is important for the Brunner good-faith prong: you must show you tried IDR, not that IDR was impossible.

Private Student Loans in Washington

Private student loans are treated differently. Under the 10th Circuit's McDaniel v. Navient, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020), and similar reasoning in other circuits, a "qualified education loan" under 523(a)(8)(B) requires the funds to have been used solely for qualified educational expenses. Loans for living expenses, test preparation, or bar study may be dischargeable without proving undue hardship.

For Washington debtors with private loans:

Direct-to-consumer (DTC) loans - often exceed "cost of attendance" and may be fully dischargeable.

Bar study loans - typically dischargeable under In re Campbell / McDaniel reasoning.

Mixed-use loans - fact-specific; the burden is on the creditor to prove qualified-loan status.

See private student loan dischargeability.

Washington Chapter 13 and Student Loans

In Chapter 13, student loans are generally paid pro-rata with other unsecured debt through the plan under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(1). The debtor may still file an adversary proceeding for discharge on undue hardship grounds, either during the case or after plan completion.

Practical advantages of the Chapter 13 path in Washington:

The automatic stay halts collection during the 3-5 year plan.

Accrued interest may be reduced through plan treatment.

A post-plan discharge adversary may succeed where a pre-plan one would not, because a completed plan is strong good-faith evidence.

See Chapter 13 and student loans.

Attorney Fees for Washington Adversary Proceedings

Student loan adversary proceedings carry fees in addition to the base Chapter 7 or 13 attorney fee. Typical Washington range: $2,000-$6,000 depending on case complexity and whether the loan holder contests discharge.

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 329(b), the bankruptcy court may review any attorney fee paid "in connection with" the case, including adversary-proceeding fees. Any fee paid for student loan litigation must be disclosed under Rule 2016(b) and is subject to the reasonableness standard. See Section 329 fee disgorgement overview.

Related Washington Resources

McDaniel v. Navient Solutions, LLC, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020) - private student loans outside Section 523(a)(8) scope.

Rosenberg v. New York State Higher Educ. Servs. Corp., 610 B.R. 454 (S.D.N.Y. 2020) - seminal post-Brunner critique; catalyst for the 2022 DOJ attestation guidance.

Long v. Educational Credit Mgmt. Corp., 322 F.3d 549 (8th Cir. 2003) - totality-of-circumstances alternative.

## Student Loan Bankruptcy in West Virginia [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR
Source: https://bankruptcystudentloans.org/states/west-virginia.html

← bankruptcystudentloans.org home

Student Loan Bankruptcy in West Virginia [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for West Virginia residents.

Student Loan Discharge in West Virginia

West Virginia sits in the Fourth Circuit, which applies the Brunner three-prong test. Each prong must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence in an adversary proceeding.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). To discharge them, the debtor must file an adversary proceeding within the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the test applied in the Fourth Circuit.

The Fourth Circuit Brunner Standard

Applies Brunner. In re Frushour, 433 F.3d 393 (4th Cir. 2005). Strict good-faith inquiry; debtors expected to document IBR/IDR attempts.

Brunner (where it applies) requires the debtor to prove:

Minimal standard of living. That the debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and dependents if forced to repay the loans.

Persistence. That additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. That the debtor has made good faith efforts to repay the loans (including IDR/IBR enrollment, forbearances attempted, and payment history).

See the full Brunner test explanation.

In November 2022, the Department of Justice and Department of Education issued joint guidance that streamlines student loan discharge for federal loans. The guidance applies in every federal court, including those in West Virginia, and has materially increased discharge success rates.

Under the attestation process:

The debtor completes a standardized DOJ attestation form documenting income, expenses, and repayment history.

The DOJ reviews the attestation and, in most cases, supports discharge rather than contesting.

The underlying Brunner/totality analysis is applied, but with DOJ alignment.

The U.S. Trustee in West Virginia processes adversary proceedings consistent with this guidance. See adversary proceeding mechanics.

West Virginia Disability and TPD Discharge

WV Rural Health Initiative; federal TPD. For Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) or Social Security Supplemental Security Income (SSI) recipients, federal loans qualify for Total and Permanent Disability (TPD) discharge without bankruptcy. TPD is administrative - no adversary proceeding needed - and applies to federal Direct, FFEL, and Perkins loans.

TPD is the first path to check for any West Virginia debtor with a disability. Bankruptcy discharge is the fallback when TPD is unavailable or for private loans.

West Virginia Income-Driven Repayment Baseline

Before filing an adversary proceeding, most courts in the Fourth Circuit require the debtor to show they have attempted income-driven repayment (IDR). Below-median; federal TPD primary disability path.

Federal IDR plans available:

SAVE (formerly REPAYE) - 5-10% of discretionary income; lowest monthly payments for most debtors.

PAYE - 10% of discretionary income; 20-year forgiveness.

IBR - 10-15% of discretionary income; 20-25 year forgiveness.

ICR - 20% of discretionary income or 12-year standard, whichever less.

A West Virginia debtor at poverty-line income typically has a $0 monthly IDR payment under SAVE. This is important for the Brunner good-faith prong: you must show you tried IDR, not that IDR was impossible.

Private Student Loans in West Virginia

Private student loans are treated differently. Under the 10th Circuit's McDaniel v. Navient, 973 F.3d 1083 (10th Cir. 2020), and similar reasoning in other circuits, a "qualified education loan" under 523(a)(8)(B) requires the funds to have been used solely for qualified educational expenses. Loans for living expenses, test preparation, or bar study may be dischargeable without proving undue hardship.

For West Virginia debtors with private loans:

Direct-to-consumer (DTC) loans - often exceed "cost of attendance" and may be fully dischargeable.

Bar study loans - typically dischargeable under In re Campbell / McDaniel reasoning.

Mixed-use loans - fact-specific; the burden is on the creditor to prove qualified-loan status.

See private student loan dischargeability.

West Virginia Federal Bankruptcy Data

Student loan adversary proceedings are filed within an underlying Chapter 7 or 13 case. The West Virginia consumer bankruptcy volume below shows the size of the pool where a 523(a)(8) complaint could be brought.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 60 consumer bankruptcy cases from West Virginia's federal bankruptcy courts.

West Virginia Chapter 13 and Student Loans

In Chapter 13, student loans are generally paid pro-rata with other unsecured debt through the plan under 11 U.S.C. Section 1322(b)(1). The debtor may still file an adversary proceeding for discharge on undue hardship grounds, either during the case or after plan completion.

Practical advantages of the Chapter 13 path in West Virginia:

The automatic stay halts collection during the 3-5 year plan.

Accrued interest may be reduced through plan treatment.

A post-plan discharge adversary may succeed where a pre-plan one would not, because a completed plan is strong good-faith evidence.

Student loan adversary proceedings carry fees in addition to the base Chapter 7 or 13 attorney fee. Typical West Virginia range: $2,000-$6,000 depending on case complexity and whether the loan holder contests discharge.

## Student Loan Bankruptcy in Wisconsin [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR
Source: https://bankruptcystudentloans.org/states/wisconsin.html

← bankruptcystudentloans.org home

Student Loan Bankruptcy in Wisconsin [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Wisconsin residents.

Student Loan Discharge in Wisconsin

Wisconsin sits in the Seventh Circuit, which applies the Brunner three-prong test. Each prong must be proven by a preponderance of the evidence in an adversary proceeding.

Student loans are presumptively non-dischargeable under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(8). To discharge them, the debtor must file an adversary proceeding within the bankruptcy case and prove undue hardship under the test applied in the Seventh Circuit.

The Seventh Circuit Brunner Standard

Applies Brunner. In re Roberson, 999 F.2d 1132 (7th Cir. 1993). Partial discharges available under In re Saxman-style reasoning.

Brunner (where it applies) requires the debtor to prove:

Minimal standard of living. That the debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and dependents if forced to repay the loans.

Persistence. That additional circumstances indicate this state of affairs will persist for a significant portion of the repayment period.

Good faith. That the debtor has made good faith efforts to repay the loans (including IDR/IBR enrollment, forbearances attempted, and payment history).

See the full Brunner test explanation.

Federal IDR plans available:

SAVE (formerly REPAYE) - 5-10% of discretionary income; lowest monthly payments for most debtors.

## Student Loan Bankruptcy in Wyoming [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR
Source: https://bankruptcystudentloans.org/states/wyoming.html

← bankruptcystudentloans.org home

Student Loan Bankruptcy in Wyoming [2026]: Brunner, TPD, and IDR

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Wyoming residents.

Student Loan Discharge in Wyoming

The Tenth Circuit Brunner Standard

Applies Brunner. In re Woodcock, 45 F.3d 363 (10th Cir. 1995). Recent panels have loosened the good-faith prong; see McDaniel v. Navient (2020) on tuition-vs-educational distinction.

Brunner (where it applies) requires the debtor to prove:

Minimal standard of living. That the debtor cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for themselves and dependents if forced to repay the loans.

## Additional FAQ Pages


### Can I discharge student loans in bankruptcy? - Student Loans in Bankruptcy
Source: https://bankruptcystudentloans.org/paa/can-i-discharge-student-loans-in-bankruptcy.html

Skip to content

bankruptcystudentloans.org

Home
Questions

Home › Common Questions › Can I discharge student loans in bankruptcy?

People Also Ask

Can I discharge student loans in bankruptcy?

Yes, but it requires filing a separate lawsuit called an adversary proceeding within your bankruptcy case. You must prove that repaying the loans would cause 'undue hardship.' Recent DOJ guidance has made this easier, and courts are increasingly willing to discharge student loans, especially for borrowers with health issues or low earning potential.

Student loan discharge in bankruptcy is harder than discharging other debts, but it is not impossible - and it is getting easier.

The Adversary Proceeding

Unlike credit cards or medical bills, student loans are not automatically discharged when you file bankruptcy. You must file a separate adversary proceeding (essentially a lawsuit within your bankruptcy case) specifically asking the court to discharge your student loans. This requires filing a complaint, serving it on the lender, and potentially going to trial.

The Undue Hardship Standard

Most courts use one of two tests:

Brunner Test: Used by most circuits. You must show (1) you cannot maintain a minimal standard of living and repay the loans, (2) your financial situation is likely to persist for a significant part of the repayment period, and (3) you have made good faith efforts to repay.

Totality of Circumstances: Used by the 8th Circuit and gaining traction elsewhere. The court looks at your complete financial picture without rigid prongs.

2023 DOJ Guidance

The Department of Justice issued new guidance in 2023 directing government attorneys to consent to discharge in cases where the borrower clearly meets the undue hardship standard. This has led to more settlements and fewer contested cases, reducing the cost and difficulty for borrowers.

Who Has the Best Chance?

Borrowers with disabilities, chronic health conditions, older borrowers with limited earning potential, and those with private student loans (which lack income-driven repayment options) have the strongest cases. But even younger borrowers with federal loans have succeeded when their financial circumstances are genuinely dire.

People Also Ask

Can private student loans be discharged in bankruptcy?

Private student loans face the same 'undue hardship' standard as federal loans, but borrowers may have a stronger case because private loans lack income-driven repayment options, deferment programs, and Public Service Loan Forgiveness. Courts increasingly recognize that the absence of these protections supports a finding of undue hardship.

Private student loans are treated the same as federal loans under the Bankruptcy Code, but the practical arguments for discharge can be stronger.

Why Private Loans May Be Easier to Discharge

Federal student loans come with numerous repayment alternatives: income-driven repayment (IDR), deferment, forbearance, Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF), and disability discharge. Private loans offer few or none of these options. Courts have recognized that the lack of repayment flexibility supports a finding of undue hardship.

Additional Arguments for Private Loan Discharge

Private loans often carry higher interest rates (8-15% vs. 5-7% for federal)

Some private loans were made to students at schools that provided little value or later closed

Co-signer disputes and aggressive collection practices may support bad-faith arguments against lenders

Many private lenders lack proper documentation of the original loan terms

The Bar Program Exception

Some private educational loans may not actually qualify for the bankruptcy discharge exception under Section 523(a)(8). The statute requires that the loan be a "qualified education loan" under the Internal Revenue Code. Loans that exceed the cost of attendance, loans to non-accredited schools, or certain refinanced loans may not meet this definition - making them dischargeable without proving undue hardship at all.

If you have private student loans and are considering bankruptcy, it is worth consulting an attorney who specializes in student loan discharge. The legal landscape has shifted significantly in borrowers' favor.

Understanding Your Bankruptcy Options

Bankruptcy law provides several paths to financial relief, each designed for different situations. Chapter 7 offers a fresh start through liquidation of non-exempt assets and discharge of qualifying debts, typically completed in 3 to 6 months. Chapter 13 allows you to keep your property while repaying debts over 3 to 5 years. Chapter 11 provides reorganization options for businesses and high-debt individuals. Understanding which chapter fits your situation requires analyzing your income, assets, debts, and financial goals.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are the different types of bankruptcy?

The most common types are Chapter 7 (liquidation for individuals and businesses), Chapter 13 (repayment plan for individuals with regular income), and Chapter 11 (reorganization for businesses). Each chapter has different eligibility requirements, timelines, and outcomes. A bankruptcy attorney or legal aid organization can help determine which option fits your situation.

How much does it cost to file bankruptcy?

Court filing fees are $338 for Chapter 7 and $313 for Chapter 13 as of 2026. Attorney fees vary by location and complexity but typically range from $1,000 to $2,500 for Chapter 7 and $2,500 to $5,000 for Chapter 13. Fee waivers are available for filers below 150% of the federal poverty guidelines.

Will bankruptcy stop creditor calls and lawsuits?

Yes. The automatic stay under 11 U.S.C. Section 362 takes effect immediately when you file and stops most collection activities, including phone calls, letters, lawsuits, wage garnishments, and foreclosure or repossession actions. Creditors who violate the stay can be held in contempt of court.

### What is the Brunner test for student loans? - Student Loans in Bankruptcy
Source: https://bankruptcystudentloans.org/paa/what-is-the-brunner-test-for-student-loans.html

Skip to content

bankruptcystudentloans.org

Home
Questions

Home › Common Questions › What is the Brunner test for student loans?

People Also Ask

What is the Brunner test for student loans?

The Brunner test is a three-part legal standard that courts use to determine if student loans can be discharged in bankruptcy. You must prove: (1) you cannot maintain a minimal standard of living and repay the loans, (2) your financial hardship is likely to persist, and (3) you have made good-faith efforts to repay.

The Brunner test comes from the 1987 case Brunner v. New York State Higher Education Services Corp. and remains the dominant standard in most federal circuits.

The Three Prongs

Prong 1: Current Inability to Pay

You must demonstrate that based on your current income and expenses, you cannot maintain a minimal standard of living for yourself and your dependents while repaying the student loans. "Minimal standard of living" does not mean poverty - courts have recognized that basic necessities include housing, food, utilities, transportation, and healthcare.

Prong 2: Persistence of Hardship

You must show that additional circumstances exist indicating your financial situation is likely to persist for a significant portion of the remaining repayment period. This is often demonstrated through age, disability, chronic health conditions, limited education or skills, or a depressed job market in your field.

Prong 3: Good Faith Effort

You must show that you have made good faith efforts to repay the loans. This does not require perfect payment history. Enrolling in income-driven repayment plans, making some payments, communicating with servicers, and exploring repayment options all demonstrate good faith.

Criticism and Reform

The Brunner test has been widely criticized as too rigid. Some courts have moved to a more flexible "totality of the circumstances" approach. The 2023 DOJ guidance has also softened enforcement. The legal landscape is shifting in borrowers' favor, and more attorneys are willing to take these cases than ever before.
